author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a corn snake itself cost?
faqs.a: A normal morph runs $25 to $70. Rare or designer morphs climb into the hundreds or occasionally low thousands, but the animal itself is the cheap part of ownership either way.

faqs.q: Is a thermostat necessary for a corn snake?
faqs.a: Yes, non-optional. A heat mat running without one can reach around 120°F, hot enough to cause a serious burn. Budget $30 to $100 for a quality thermostat as part of your core setup, not an add-on.

faqs.q: What does a corn snake cost per year after the initial setup?
faqs.a: Most owners land around $200 to $500 a year: frozen mice ($10-20 a month), substrate ($30-80 a year), electricity for the heat source ($60-180 a year), and an annual wellness exam ($50-150).

faqs.q: What's the total cost over a corn snake's lifetime?
faqs.a: 15 to 20 years is typical in captivity, and the oldest verified corn snake reached 32. Across ten years, setup and every running expense together usually total $800 to $2,000, which is cheap for a reptile you keep that long.

title: Corn Snake Enrichment: The Species With the Most Research Behind It
seoTitle: Corn Snake Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Given an enclosure longer than their own body, corn snakes stretch all the way out and prefer it. That single result kills the oldest myth in snake keeping.
imageAlt: A corn snake stretched out across a branch in a planted enclosure
author: Mike

faqs.q: Do corn snakes prefer a bigger enclosure?
faqs.a: Yes, and it has been tested. Hoehfurtner and colleagues housed corn snakes in enclosures either two thirds of their body length or longer than their body length. Given the opportunity to stretch out fully, the snakes did so, and they showed a clear preference for the larger enclosure. The authors recommend enclosures that allow a snake to stretch.

faqs.q: Is a bigger tank enrichment, or just better housing?
faqs.a: For this species the research treats it as both. Floor space is what makes stretching, exploring and using multiple microclimates possible at all, so it functions as the enabling condition for almost every other enrichment item rather than as a separate category.

faqs.q: Does enrichment change anything measurable in corn snakes?
faqs.a: A separate 2021 study found that environmental enrichment affected corn snakes' ability to discriminate between familiar and unfamiliar human odors, which is a cognitive outcome rather than just an activity count. Earlier work by Almli and Burghardt on ratsnakes, the group corn snakes belong to, found enriched housing altered their behavioral profile and performance on problem solving and feeding tasks.

faqs.q: Do corn snakes climb?
faqs.a: Readily. They are semi-arboreal in the wild and will use branches, cork and any stable elevated structure you provide. A tall enclosure is less useful than a long one, but adding height on top of adequate floor space is well used.

faqs.q: What is the lowest-effort enrichment that works?
faqs.a: Scent. Corn snakes navigate chemically, so a shed skin from another enclosure, a scent-marked object, or dragging prey across the substrate before offering it gives them something to investigate with their primary sense. It costs nothing.

faqs.q: Will a hiding snake in a large enclosure be stressed?
faqs.a: Not if the enclosure has cover throughout. The mistake is giving a snake more space without giving it more places to be concealed, which produces an animal that uses only the two hides. Clutter the whole floor and the space gets used.

title: Corn Snake Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and Why They Stop Eating
seoTitle: What Do Corn Snakes Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: How often to feed a corn snake by age and weight, why frozen/thawed beats live prey, and the honest range of reasons corn snakes go off food, from a normal shed to brumation.
imageAlt: Corn snake investigating a properly thawed mouse in its enclosure
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How often should I feed my corn snake?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on age and weight, not just age alone. Hatchlings under about 3 months eat every 5 to 7 days, working down to every 14 to 21 days for a fully mature adult. A vet-content source gives more frequent numbers across the board, every other day for babies, every 1 to 2 weeks for adults, so there's real disagreement here, but the specialist reptile-care consensus is the more frequent, evenly-converged figure worth following.

faqs.q: Is frozen/thawed prey better than live prey?
faqs.a: Yes, and by a wide margin. Live rodents can bite, scratch, or claw a snake that isn't hungry enough to strike immediately, sometimes causing serious infection. Frozen/thawed removes that risk entirely and is the standard recommendation across every source consulted.

faqs.q: Does my corn snake need calcium or vitamin supplements?
faqs.a: Generally no. A normal whole-prey diet, bones and organs included, provides complete nutrition for a corn snake, unlike insect-eating reptiles. Some sources recommend light dusting for hatchlings specifically on pinky mice, tapering off once the snake moves to larger prey, but over-supplementing calcium can itself cause problems.

faqs.q: Why has my corn snake stopped eating?
faqs.a: Most commonly it's shedding, brumation, or, in males especially, breeding-season restlessness, all normal. It becomes a concern when it's paired with weight loss, lethargy, respiratory signs, or when the enclosure's warm side isn't warm enough for the snake to digest food safely.

faqs.q: How long can a corn snake go without eating?
faqs.a: Longer than most owners expect for a healthy adult, commonly cited at 2 to 3 months thanks to a slow reptile metabolism. Sources disagree on the exact threshold for concern though, one vet-content source recommends calling a vet after missing just a couple of feedings, while reptile-specialist sources say refusal isn't unusual until it passes 1 to 2 months outside of a planned brumation. Babies have far less reserve, a week without eating is worth taking seriously in a hatchling.

faqs.q: Can I feed my corn snake anything besides mice?
faqs.a: Whole prey variety is fine if you want it, young rats, quail, quail eggs, or day-old chicks are all mentioned across sources, though mice remain the default staple in the pet trade. Skip meat scraps, cooked food, and insects entirely, none of that is appropriate for this species.

title: How to Handle a Corn Snake
seoTitle: How to Handle a Corn Snake Correctly
excerpt: Corn snakes are docile and hardy as adults, but juveniles can be fast, wiggly, and defensive before they settle into the calmer temperament the species is known for.
imageAlt: Corn snake being gently supported across two hands
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How soon can I handle a new corn snake?
faqs.a: Give it time to acclimate and eat successfully 3 to 4 times first, roughly one to two weeks at minimum. For hatchlings, start with sessions as short as 1 to 2 minutes once they've settled in.

faqs.q: How often can a corn snake be handled?
faqs.a: A couple of times a week at first, 5 or 10 minutes a session. Build from there as the snake tolerates more.

faqs.q: How long should I wait to handle after feeding?
faqs.a: 48 to 72 hours. Picking a snake up on a full stomach is a leading cause of regurgitation, and the calendar is all it takes to avoid it.

faqs.q: Is it normal for a corn snake to bite or musk when handled?
faqs.a: Bites are rare and minor, typically a startled or defensive reaction rather than genuine aggression, and easily treated with soap and water. Musking, a foul-smelling defensive secretion, is a stress signal, if you see it along with tight coiling or striking, it's time to end the session calmly.

title: Common Corn Snake Health Issues and What Causes Them
seoTitle: Corn Snake Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Corn snakes are one of the hardier pet snakes, and nearly every health problem they develop traces back to husbandry rather than bad luck.
imageAlt: Corn snake coiled on a stainless steel exam table in a vet clinic
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What is the most common health problem in corn snakes?
faqs.a: Respiratory infection. It's usually bacterial, and almost always follows an enclosure that runs too cold or too damp. Watch for open-mouth breathing, clicking or wheezing, mucus at the nose or mouth, and lethargy. That combination needs a reptile vet and prescription antibiotics, not a wait-and-see approach.

faqs.q: What causes scale rot in corn snakes?
faqs.a: Damp or dirty substrate, or a water bowl that overflows or sits unchanged too long. Signs are belly scales gone brown, yellow, or black, skin that looks soft, mushy, or blistered, and a foul smell. Fix the husbandry problem and see a vet, especially if it's spreading.

faqs.q: How do I treat mites on a corn snake?
faqs.a: Treat the enclosure at the same time as the snake. Treating the snake alone lets the infestation come back. You'll see the mites as tiny black or red specks moving on the scales or floating in the water bowl.

faqs.q: What neurological signs in a corn snake need immediate attention?
faqs.a: Star-gazing, where the head is held tilted up and back, and corkscrewing movements. Both are rare but serious, and warrant an immediate vet visit.

title: Is It Legal to Own a Corn Snake? State-by-State Guide
seoTitle: Is a Corn Snake Legal in Your State? Full Guide
excerpt: Corn snakes are the classic pet-store starter snake almost everywhere, except Georgia, where the state's own wildlife agency lists them as a native species that can't be kept as a pet at all, captive-bred or not. New Jersey, South Carolina, Illinois, Maryland, and Minnesota all attach their own conditions too, and two of them work by morph name rather than by species.
imageAlt: Corn snake with its distinctive orange and black blotched pattern
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Is a corn snake banned in Georgia?
faqs.a: Yes. Georgia DNR's own Guide to Legal Pets lists corn snake among native species that "may not be held as a pet regardless of its origin or morphology," so even a captive-bred corn snake from an out-of-state breeder is treated the same as a wild-caught one. The rule is grounded in Georgia's wild animal statute, O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4 and § 27-5-5.

faqs.q: Can I own a captive-bred corn snake in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Only if it is one of nine named color morphs. The corn snake is on New Jersey's own endangered species list at N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.13(b), which under 7:25-4.10(a) means no permit may be issued for it and under 7:25-4.15(b) means it may not be kept as a pet. Fish and Wildlife then carves out captive morphs, because a morph is visibly not a wild-phase animal, and names nine that may be kept and sold: red albino, butter, blizzard, candy cane, creamsicle, lavender, pearl, snow, and sun glow. A normal-looking corn snake is barred whatever its paperwork says.

faqs.q: Is there a size limit on corn snakes in South Carolina?
faqs.a: Yes, for the specific exception that makes them legal at all. South Carolina's Act 177 generally bars possessing native reptiles, but allows corn snakes that are captive-bred and under 20 inches in total length as the one pet-trade exception to that rule.

title: Corn Snake Tank Setup: Floor Space, a Mandatory Thermostat, and a Humidity Debate
seoTitle: Corn Snake Tank Setup Guide
excerpt: Corn snakes are a forgiving species to set up correctly, with one non-negotiable exception: whatever heat source you choose, it needs a thermostat.
imageAlt: Corn snake enclosure with hides, water bowl, and climbing branches
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size enclosure does an adult corn snake need?
faqs.a: A 40-gallon breeder (36x18x18 inches) is the adult minimum, with 4x2x2 feet (48x24x24 inches) as the preferred size for a fully grown adult. Corn snakes are terrestrial, so floor space matters more than height.

faqs.q: Is a thermostat required for a corn snake enclosure?
faqs.a: Yes, with zero exceptions. An unregulated heat mat can reach roughly 120°F, hot enough to burn a snake badly. Put the probe where the snake spends its time, in the warm hide or on the substrate, not taped to the mat.

faqs.q: What humidity level does a corn snake need?
faqs.a: Sources disagree, some recommend 65-75%, others cite 40-60% as sufficient, raised to 60-70% during shedding. Either range works in practice, what matters more is consistency and a dedicated humid hide with damp sphagnum moss during shed cycles.

faqs.q: Does a corn snake need UVB?
faqs.a: Not required. Corn snakes have been kept for decades without it, though it is increasingly seen as beneficial long term. If you add one, use a low-output T5 targeting a UVI around 2.0 to 3.0.

title: Corn Snake vs. Hognose Snake: Which Beginner-Friendly Snake Fits You
seoTitle: Corn Snake vs. Hognose Snake: Beginner Snake Guide
excerpt: Corn snake or hognose snake? The differences in size, feeding, and that famous hognose 'death drop' - not just which one is trending on social media.
imageAlt: A corn snake and a hognose snake side by side for comparison
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Are hognose snakes venomous, and is that dangerous to keep as a pet?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but not in any way that matters for a pet owner. Hognoses have small rear fangs and a mild venom evolved to subdue toads, their main prey in the wild. It's not considered medically significant to humans, and captive-bred hognoses very rarely bite at all. The one documented bite case in the literature stayed local: swelling, bruising and mild cellulitis, with no systemic effects.

faqs.q: Which is easier to feed, a corn snake or a hognose snake?
faqs.a: Corn snakes, generally. They're reliable, consistent eaters of standard frozen-thawed mice. Hognoses can be pickier, since some individuals show a preference for amphibian scent from their wild toad-eating instincts, occasionally requiring a mouse to be scented to get a hesitant eater interested.

faqs.q: Which snake stays smaller, corn snake or hognose?
faqs.a: Hognose snakes, noticeably. Adult hognoses typically reach 2 to 3.5 feet, while adult corn snakes commonly reach 3.5 to 5 feet. That size difference also means a hognose can be housed comfortably in a smaller adult enclosure, especially adult males, which stay on the smaller end of that range.

faqs.q: Why does my hognose snake play dead?
faqs.a: It's a bluff, not real distress. When a hognose feels seriously threatened, it puts on a dramatic show: flattening its neck like a mini cobra, hissing, and striking with its mouth closed. If that doesn't work, it flips onto its back, opens its mouth, and goes completely limp, playing dead rather than trying to bite or flee. It's one of the most distinctive defensive behaviors of any pet snake and it essentially never leads to an actual bite.

faqs.q: Which is better for a first snake, a corn snake or a hognose snake?
faqs.a: Corn snakes are still the more universally recommended first snake, thanks to unmatched feeding reliability and decades of established beginner-friendly husbandry information. That said, hognoses have become a very popular second choice, or even a first snake for someone specifically drawn to their unusual look and famous defensive display, and their smaller adult size is a genuine point in their favor.

faqs.q: Do corn snakes or hognose snakes need higher humidity?
faqs.a: Hognoses run drier. They're an arid-preferring species at 30 to 50% ambient humidity, with just one dedicated humid hide for shedding. Corn snakes sit a bit higher, with many sources citing a 40 to 60% baseline. Neither is a high-humidity species compared to something like a ball python, but a hognose is the drier of the two by design, reflecting its native prairie and scrubland habitat.

title: How Much Does Corydoras Catfish Ownership Really Cost?
seoTitle: Corydoras Catfish Price: $3 to $30, Plus $150 to $215 Setup
excerpt: Corydoras catfish are inexpensive on their own, but the budgeting consideration isn't the individual fish, it's that you need to buy a whole school, not one or two.
imageAlt: A school of corydoras catfish foraging together over soft sand substrate
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a corydoras catfish cost?
faqs.a: $3 to $8 each for the common ones: panda, peppered, bronze, albino. Specialty species cost considerably more, with corydoras barbatus around $30 and orange laser corydoras $15 to $20. Groups of six or more are the requirement, so price the school rather than the fish.

faqs.q: What does a basic corydoras catfish tank setup cost?
faqs.a: Roughly $150 to $215 upfront, covering a 20-gallon long tank, a filter and heater, soft sand substrate, plants, hides, a water conditioner, and a test kit. The substrate line item matters more for this species than it does for most community fish.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing costs of keeping corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: Roughly $10 to $20 a month. Most of it is a sinking food they can reach at the bottom, plus water conditioner, replacement filter media, and modest electricity.

faqs.q: Do corydoras catfish need regular vet visits?
faqs.a: Aquatic vets are uncommon. Most cory health problems get handled by the keeper instead, through correcting water quality and using appropriate medication.

faqs.q: How long do corydoras catfish live?
faqs.a: 5 to 10 years is typical, and some individuals live well past that, with occasional reports of up to 15 years in ideal conditions. Plan the tank around it: that's longer than many people expect from a small bottom dweller.

faqs.q: Why do I need to budget for six fish instead of one?
faqs.a: Kept in groups smaller than six, cories are stressed and behave abnormally. The price of one corydoras is therefore the price of at least six, plus a tank big enough to hold them comfortably. Buying the full school at the start is more humane and more cost effective than adding to it later.

title: Corydoras Enrichment: Sand for the Sifting, Not for the Barbels
seoTitle: Corydoras Catfish Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Everyone says gravel wears down cory barbels. No study establishes the cause, and substrate of any kind is a documented home for pathogenic bacteria.
imageAlt: A group of corydoras catfish sifting fine sand with their barbels, snouts buried
author: Mike

faqs.q: Does gravel wear down corydoras barbels?
faqs.a: That is the standard explanation, and no controlled study establishes it, or any competing mechanism. What is documented is that substrate of any kind harbors pathogenic bacteria, so a clean substrate matters more than its grain shape, and plenty of keepers have raised healthy corydoras on smooth gravel for decades.

faqs.q: So should I use gravel?
faqs.a: Sand is still the better choice, for a different reason: corydoras are social foragers that root through the substrate with their barbels to find food, and fine sand is what lets them do it without hurting themselves. The behavioral argument for sand is stronger than the barbel argument ever was.

faqs.q: What prevents barbel erosion?
faqs.a: Keeping the bottom clean. Regular substrate vacuuming, low nitrate, no uneaten food left to rot. Sharp substrate is not ideal and is a secondary factor next to what is living in a dirty one.

faqs.q: How many corydoras should I keep?
faqs.a: Six at absolute minimum and more is better. They are social bottom-dwellers that shoal, forage and rest together, and a group of two or three is a visibly less active, more nervous set of fish.

faqs.q: Why do they dash to the surface?
faqs.a: Corydoras can gulp air and absorb oxygen through the gut, which is normal behavior rather than a symptom. It becomes a warning sign when it happens constantly, which usually means the water is low in oxygen or fouled.

faqs.q: Do they eat leftovers?
faqs.a: This is the myth that starves them. Corydoras are not a cleanup crew and will not thrive on whatever the other fish miss. They need sinking food fed for them, after lights out if faster tankmates are taking it.

title: Corydoras Catfish Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and Why They Stop Eating
seoTitle: What Do Corydoras Catfish Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: Corydoras have a reputation as an algae-eating cleanup crew that isn't accurate, and believing it is one of the easiest ways to accidentally starve a fish that otherwise asks very little of you.
imageAlt: A school of corydoras catfish feeding on sinking wafers at the bottom of the tank
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Do corydoras catfish eat algae?
faqs.a: Not effectively. Left to live off leftovers and algae film as a self-sufficient cleanup crew, a cory can slowly starve, especially alongside faster, more aggressive eaters. They need dedicated sinking food, offered on purpose every time.

faqs.q: What should I feed corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: A sinking pellet or wafer made for bottom feeders or catfish, around 30 to 40% protein, does the staple work. Worms belong in the rotation regularly: live blackworms, frozen bloodworms, or Hikari Vibra Bites, plus occasional sinking gel foods. Blanched vegetables are a side, not the main event.

faqs.q: How much and how often should I feed corydoras?
faqs.a: Once or twice daily, and only what the group clears in 2 to 3 minutes. Start at about one sinking wafer per 3 to 4 fish, or 2 to 3 small pellets each, then adjust to what gets eaten. Food still sitting there after 20 to 30 minutes means cut back next time.

faqs.q: Why shouldn't I rely on floating flakes for corydoras?
faqs.a: Because they feed on the bottom. Flakes get eaten by mid and upper-tank fish long before they sink far enough to matter, so a tank fed exclusively with flakes can leave cories functionally unfed even though food goes in daily.

faqs.q: Why has my corydoras catfish stopped eating?
faqs.a: Stress is the most common cause, including from being kept alone or in too small a group, poor water quality, especially ammonia buildup, disease, and the ordinary acclimation period after a move or a new tank are all documented causes.

faqs.q: How can I tell if poor water quality is why my cory stopped eating?
faqs.a: Test ammonia and nitrite directly rather than guessing, elevated levels are a repeatedly cited cause of both appetite loss and lethargy in this species. Bad water conditions cause real stress, and correcting water quality often resolves the appetite issue on its own.

title: Corydoras Catfish Aren't Handled, and They're Not Solo Fish Either
seoTitle: Corydoras Catfish Behavior and Handling Guide
excerpt: Corydoras catfish are an observation animal, not a hands-on one. What matters with this species is its role in a tank, and that role is a very different one from a centerpiece fish like the oscar.
imageAlt: A group of corydoras catfish schooling together low over sand substrate
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Do you handle corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: No, this is an observation fish. What matters is the role it plays in a tank: small, peaceful, and working the bottom, with no hands-on interaction involved.

faqs.q: Are corydoras catfish algae eaters?
faqs.a: No, the cleanup crew reputation is wrong. Cories pick leftover food off the bottom, which helps but isn't the same job, and they need sinking food of their own. Algae and scraps won't keep them alive.

faqs.q: How many corydoras catfish need to be kept together?
faqs.a: Six of the same species, minimum. A lone or paired cory hides, darts erratically, and goes off its food, which is what an inadequate group looks like. Treat the number as a welfare requirement.

faqs.q: Why does my corydoras dart to the surface for air?
faqs.a: It's an adaptation that supplements gill breathing, and in moderation it's completely normal. It doesn't mean the water is short on oxygen. Knowing that ahead of time keeps you from misreading it as distress.

faqs.q: What mistakes do first-time corydoras owners make?
faqs.a: Buying three or four instead of a school of six. Choosing sharp substrate, which damages this species' sensitive barbels. And picking tankmates that nip fins or are big enough to eat a cory.

faqs.q: How does keeping corydoras compare to keeping an oscar?
faqs.a: Opposite ends of a tank. An oscar is a large, assertive centerpiece the whole setup gets planned around, while cories are small, peaceful bottom dwellers filling a supporting role in a community.

title: Common Corydoras Catfish Health Issues
seoTitle: Corydoras Catfish Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Corydoras catfish are sensitive to two things above all else, substrate texture and water quality, and understanding that connection explains most of what shows up on this list.
imageAlt: Close-up of a corydoras catfish foraging over sand substrate, showing its barbels
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What is barbel erosion in corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: The barbels, those whisker-like feelers around the mouth, wear down: shortened, red, or gone entirely. It's the signature cory health issue. Sharp substrate is the usual explanation, and eroding barbels may owe as much to poor water quality as to grain shape, so a dirty substrate is what to manage first.

faqs.q: Can barbel erosion be treated at home?
faqs.a: Yes, if it's caught reasonably early. Move to soft sand, do a significant water change, and hold nitrates under 20 ppm from there on. Barbels can regrow over 4 to 8 weeks once conditions improve. Untreated, it can progress to red blotch disease.

faqs.q: What is red blotch disease?
faqs.a: Sores on the belly and flanks that look red or bloody. It's often linked to a bacterial infection, and the stress of shipping or a new environment frequently triggers it. Treat it early: fix water quality and use a broad-spectrum antibiotic, often at half the standard dose for this species.

faqs.q: How do you treat ich in corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: Raise the temperature gradually toward 82°F with strong aeration, and reduce the medication dose. This species doesn't tolerate a full-strength treatment the way many hardier fish do.

faqs.q: Why are corydoras catfish more medication sensitive than other fish?
faqs.a: They're armored catfish with sensitive, naked bellies, and notably more medication sensitive than many community fish. That means reduced doses, sometimes a half or a quarter of the standard amount, and no full-strength copper, malachite green, or formalin, which this species tolerates poorly.

faqs.q: How can I prevent most corydoras catfish health issues?
faqs.a: Substrate and water quality. A clean, soft bottom and low nitrates are what keep barbel erosion away, the most defining health risk, and poor water quality plus general stress is what drives red blotch disease and fin rot. Get both right and nearly everything here is prevented.

title: Corydoras Catfish Tank Setup: Substrate Is the Detail That Actually Matters
seoTitle: Corydoras Catfish Tank Setup Guide
excerpt: Corydoras catfish are easy to house well once you get one specific decision right, what's on the bottom of the tank. Everything else about this species' care is fairly standard community-fish practice.
imageAlt: A corydoras catfish tank with soft sand substrate and a school foraging near the bottom
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size tank do corydoras catfish need?
faqs.a: A 20-gallon long is the practical minimum for a school of six standard-sized cories; dwarf and pygmy species manage in about 10 gallons. Going to 29 or 30 gallons is better, especially for a group of 8 to 15.

faqs.q: What temperature do corydoras catfish need?
faqs.a: 72 to 78°F covers most species in the hobby, though preferences vary: some take warmer water, others want it cooler. Unless the room stays warm year-round, run a reliable heater, and hold the number steady rather than chasing a precise one.

faqs.q: What water parameters do corydoras catfish need?
faqs.a: pH 7.0 to 7.8 for captive-bred cories, which is most of what the trade sells. Keep ammonia and nitrite at zero and nitrate low with regular water changes.

faqs.q: What substrate is safe for corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: Soft sand, or smooth, fine, rounded gravel, about 2 inches deep. Sharp or coarse gravel is out, and so are certain specialty planted-tank sands: manufacturers flag some sharp-grained options as unsuitable for bottom-dwellers like cories.

faqs.q: Do corydoras catfish need special lighting?
faqs.a: Standard community lighting. Cories are most active at dawn and dusk, so give them shaded cover and hides to retreat into when the tank is bright.

faqs.q: What's the non-obvious tank setup requirement for corydoras catfish?
faqs.a: Gentle water movement with calm areas to rest in, rather than one strong current everywhere. They also need clear access to the surface, since they gulp air periodically as part of normal breathing.

title: How Much Does a Crested Gecko Really Cost?
seoTitle: Crested Gecko Price: $50 to $200, Plus $335 to $530 Setup
excerpt: Crested geckos sit near the affordable end of the reptile hobby, and unlike heat-hungry desert species, most of the ongoing cost is food and humidity, not electricity.
imageAlt: Crested gecko in a fully equipped vertical arboreal enclosure
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a crested gecko itself cost?
faqs.a: $50 to $200 for a normal morph, climbing toward $500 to $1,000+ for rare, sought-after morphs.

faqs.q: Does a crested gecko need expensive heating equipment?
faqs.a: Not usually, one of its budget advantages. Many rooms already sit in a crested gecko's comfortable range, so heating is often a light supplement (a 25-40 watt bulb, $20-40) rather than a heavy setup, and electricity costs stay minimal.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing monthly costs for a crested gecko?
faqs.a: Roughly $31 to $52 a month. A complete crested gecko diet powder runs about $7 a month averaged out (one $20 bag lasts about three months), plus occasional live insects, substrate replacement, electricity, and amortized UVB bulb and vet costs.

faqs.q: How long do crested geckos live, and how does that affect budgeting?
faqs.a: 15 to 20 years in captivity, with the earliest known captive individuals living into their 30s. This isn't a short-term pet, so the setup you buy now should be one you're comfortable maintaining for decades, not just the first year.

title: Crested Gecko Enrichment: Vertical Space, Cover, and Foraging
seoTitle: Crested Gecko Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Crested geckos are arboreal, so enrichment here is mostly vertical: a real climbing network, cover at height, and food they have to find instead of a dish on the floor.
imageAlt: A crested gecko perched on a branch surrounded by foliage and cork tube hides
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What counts as enrichment for a crested gecko?
faqs.a: A complex vertical climbing network, cover at different heights so the gecko can choose how exposed it is, and food presented in a way that involves some searching or hunting rather than a static dish on the floor. It never replaces correct humidity, temperature, and a properly sized vertical enclosure, those come first.

faqs.q: Does a crested gecko need live plants?
faqs.a: Live plants aren't strictly required, high-quality artificial foliage covers the same need for daytime cover and security. Pothos, philodendron, and bromeliads are common safe choices if you do go live, and either way, dense cover reduces stress by letting the gecko control its own light exposure.

faqs.q: How much climbing structure is too much?
faqs.a: It's hard to overdo vertical complexity for this species, crested geckos are strong jumpers and use open gaps between perches on purpose. The limit is stability, every branch and piece of cork has to be anchored so nothing collapses under the gecko's weight mid-jump.

faqs.q: Is a bioactive setup necessary for enrichment?
faqs.a: No, it's an advanced option, not a requirement. A well-set-up bioactive enclosure with springtails and isopods adds continuous low-level stimulation through a growing, self-cleaning environment, but a non-bioactive setup with good climbing structure, cover, and varied feeding covers the basics just fine.

faqs.q: Should I rearrange the enclosure often for novelty?
faqs.a: Only occasionally. Sudden total overhauls of a shy individual's enclosure cause stress rather than enrichment. Small changes, a new branch angle or rotated plant, are enough, and the core climbing structure and hides are better left stable.

title: Crested Gecko Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and Why They Stop Eating
seoTitle: What Do Crested Geckos Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: Why powdered crested gecko diet, not live insects, should be the actual staple, and how to tell a picky eater from a gecko that needs help.
imageAlt: Crested gecko licking powdered crested gecko diet from a small dish
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How often should I feed my crested gecko?
faqs.a: Hatchlings and juveniles get commercial crested gecko diet (CGD) daily, with live insects added once or twice a week mostly for enrichment. Adults move to CGD every 2 to 3 days, with live insects offered about once a week.

faqs.q: Should I feed live insects or powdered CGD?
faqs.a: CGD should be the actual nutritional foundation, insects are a supplemental extra, not the base diet. Introducing insects before a gecko is reliably eating CGD is a real mistake, geckos can learn to hold out for insects and refuse the complete diet, risking malnutrition.

faqs.q: Why is my crested gecko refusing its food?
faqs.a: Often it's simple pickiness, cresties are notably fussier than most keepers expect, and may reject one flavor or texture while readily eating another. Rotating 2 to 3 CGD brands or flavors is the standard fix, one brand's watermelon flavor is specifically called out as unusually well accepted by picky eaters.

faqs.q: Do crested geckos brumate?
faqs.a: No, and they shouldn't be put through a deliberate cooling cycle the way some temperate reptiles are. That said, keepers do report cresties eating and moving less in winter months due to internal seasonal rhythms, even with stable husbandry.

faqs.q: How long can a crested gecko go without eating?
faqs.a: About 2 to 3 weeks for a healthy adult at a good weight, though a vet consult is worth considering once the second week passes, especially alongside visible weight loss. Juveniles hold far less reserve and don't get that grace period. Water runs on a shorter clock: roughly 3 days.

faqs.q: What foods are dangerous for crested geckos?
faqs.a: Avocado, citrus fruits, rhubarb, and any wild-caught insects. Fireflies are toxic and should never be fed. Onion, garlic, and eggplant are also flagged as unsafe.

title: How to Handle a Crested Gecko (And Why Tail Loss Is Different Here)
seoTitle: How to Handle a Crested Gecko Correctly
excerpt: Crested geckos are gentle and easy to handle once settled, but unlike leopard geckos, a dropped tail never grows back, which changes how carefully you should handle one.
imageAlt: Crested gecko walking from one open hand to another
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How soon can I handle a new crested gecko?
faqs.a: Two weeks after it arrives, once it has acclimated and is eating normally. Then wait for size: a sub-adult of 8 to 15 grams, roughly 4 to 5 inches at about 6 months old.

faqs.q: Does a crested gecko's tail grow back if it drops?
faqs.a: No, and this is the critical difference from species like leopard geckos. A crested gecko's tail does not grow back once dropped. The good news is a tailless gecko, often called a "frog butt" by keepers, lives a completely normal, healthy life.

faqs.q: What's the correct technique for picking up a crested gecko?
faqs.a: Let it walk onto your hand instead of reaching for it. Keepers call the trick treadmilling: cup your free hand ahead of the gecko as it reaches the edge of the other one, and it crosses over on its own.

faqs.q: How often can a crested gecko be handled?
faqs.a: One or two minutes every other day to start. Work up to around 15 minutes as the gecko gets tame, and keep the daily total under about 20 minutes.

title: Common Crested Gecko Health Issues and What Causes Them
seoTitle: Crested Gecko Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Nearly every crested gecko health problem traces back to calcium, humidity, and substrate choices. Get those right and most of this list never shows up.
imageAlt: Crested gecko being weighed on a gram scale during a health check
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What is the first sign of metabolic bone disease in a crested gecko?
faqs.a: A soft or rubbery lower jaw is often the first thing owners notice. Advanced signs include floppy or weak limbs, a visibly misaligned jaw, a kinked spine, tremors, and difficulty climbing. It's caused by a deficiency in calcium or vitamin D3, and prevention is straightforward: a complete diet powder, calcium supplementation, and low-level UVB.

faqs.q: What is floppy tail syndrome?
faqs.a: The tail drapes over the head, or sits at an odd angle to the body. It typically comes from chronic upside-down resting against glass. Because it's sometimes associated with calcium or pelvic issues, a vet visit is worth it to rule out an underlying problem.

faqs.q: What causes impaction in crested geckos?
faqs.a: Usually loose substrate like sand or bark, prey too large to pass, or shed skin left behind. Signs are no bowel movement in a week or more, a bloated abdomen, straining, and appetite loss. Solid substrate, paper towel or tile, helps prevent it in young geckos.

faqs.q: How often should I weigh my crested gecko?
faqs.a: Weekly. Weight change is often the earliest sign something's off, well before other symptoms appear, which makes a gram scale one of the most useful tools for this species.

title: Why Humidity Is Everything for Crested Geckos
excerpt: Crested geckos need a daily humidity swing, not constant dampness: a spike after the evening mist, a dry-down by afternoon. Here is the cycle, the schedule, and what goes wrong at both ends.
imageAlt: Crested gecko in a lush, humid tropical terrarium with visible mist and condensation
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What happens if humidity gets too high instead of too low?
faqs.a: Mold, and with it the bacterial or fungal infections and respiratory disease that follow. Mist less and open the vents rather than sealing the tank tighter. A gecko breathing with its mouth open needs a vet.

faqs.q: Do crested geckos need a bioactive setup for good humidity?
faqs.a: No, bioactive helps but isn't required. A well-planted enclosure with the right substrate and a consistent misting routine can hold proper humidity just as well; bioactive mainly reduces how often you need to intervene manually.

faqs.q: Do live plants help maintain humidity better than fake plants?
faqs.a: Yes, to a meaningful degree. Live plants continuously release moisture through transpiration and their soil holds humidity longer than bare substrate, which smooths out the swings between mistings. Quality fake plants still hold surface moisture fine, just without that extra ongoing contribution.

faqs.q: Can I rely on an automatic mister alone?
faqs.a: For most keepers, yes, once it's dialed in correctly. Automatic mist systems remove the inconsistency of manual spraying. Check readings with a hygrometer for the first few weeks to confirm the timer settings are hitting your target range.

faqs.q: Is a hygrometer necessary for a small enclosure?
faqs.a: Yes. You cannot see humidity, and a dial gauge lies in wet air. A digital probe tells you whether the evening spike and the afternoon dry-down both happened, which is the whole point of the cycle.

title: Is It Legal to Own a Crested Gecko? State-by-State Guide
seoTitle: Are Crested Geckos Legal? The Six Places They Aren't
excerpt: Crested geckos clear 45 of 52 jurisdictions without a permit, which makes the seven exceptions worth knowing precisely. The one most keepers never see coming is Massachusetts, where the permit is triggered by the species' conservation status rather than by anything it does.
imageAlt: Crested gecko gripping a branch, showing the eyelash crests it is named for
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to own a crested gecko?
faqs.a: In 45 of 52 US jurisdictions, no. Massachusetts, New Jersey and West Virginia all require one, Minnesota and Maine attach conditions rather than a flat clearance, and Hawaii and the District of Columbia do not allow private ownership at all. Nowhere else that was checked asks for paperwork.

faqs.q: Why does Massachusetts treat crested geckos differently from leopard geckos?
faqs.a: Massachusetts clears the gecko family without a permit, but that clearance is expressly subject to 321 CMR 9.01(3), which pulls back out anything rare. The IUCN assesses the crested gecko as vulnerable, which makes it categorically non-exempt. The leopard gecko is assessed as least concern, so the same rule leaves it alone.

faqs.q: Is the crested gecko named in Hawaii's ban?
faqs.a: No, and that is what makes it a ban. Hawaii allows introduction only for animals on its conditionally approved or restricted lists, so an animal on neither is barred by default. The crested gecko appears on no Hawaii list under either of its names, while a congener does appear, which suggests the geckos were worked through one at a time and this one was never reached.

title: Crested Gecko Tank Setup: Vertical Space, Humidity, and a Hard Temperature Ceiling
seoTitle: Crested Gecko Tank Setup Guide
excerpt: Crested geckos flip the usual reptile setup logic. Where most lizards need a hot basking spot, this species needs you to actively avoid overheating them.
imageAlt: Vertical crested gecko enclosure with branches, vines, and foliage
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size enclosure does a crested gecko need?
faqs.a: 18x18x24 inches is the minimum for one adult, and taller is better, a 2x2x2 foot enclosure is a common upgrade. Crested geckos are arboreal, so height matters more than floor space here.

faqs.q: What's the maximum safe temperature for a crested gecko enclosure?
faqs.a: 85°F, a hard ceiling with zero exceptions. New Caledonia, where they come from, tops out at 79-85°F in the hot season, and a long stretch above that risks fatal heat stroke. Too much heat is the bigger danger with this species.

faqs.q: What humidity does a crested gecko need?
faqs.a: 60 to 80%, with a daily swing: it spikes to 80% or higher right after the evening mist and dries to around 45 to 50% by late afternoon. That swing prevents mold while still giving your gecko what it needs, maintained with a daily evening misting session.

faqs.q: Does a crested gecko need UVB?
faqs.a: Not strictly, since a complete diet powder supplies vitamin D3, though low-level UVB is still a good idea. If you add it, keep it low: a 24-inch T5 HO around 5.0, for a UVI of 1.0 to 2.0.

title: Crocodiles Survived What Killed the Dinosaurs, and Not by Staying the Same
seoTitle: How Crocodiles Outlived the Dinosaurs
excerpt: Crocodilians came through the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs. The reasons are specific, and the popular idea that they did it by never changing is wrong.
imageAlt: A crocodile lying half submerged at the edge of a muddy river, eyes and snout above the waterline
author: Michael Ryan
myth: Crocodiles survived the asteroid by never changing.
truth: They changed a great deal. What carried them through was being small, aquatic, and able to go a long time without eating.

title: Crows Are Smarter Than You Think (And They Probably Already Know It)
seoTitle: How Smart Are Crows? Crow Intelligence Explained
excerpt: Crows recognize human faces, make their own tools, and hold grudges for generations. The science of crow intelligence is wilder than you think.
imageAlt: A close-up portrait of an American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos) perched on a branch, its glossy black feathers and sharp intelligent eyes in sharp focus against a softly blurred background
author: Michael Ryan
myth: Betty the crow bending a wire into a hook was the clearest case of invention in any animal.
truth: Wild New Caledonian crows bend twigs using the same motion. She applied a species-typical move to an unfamiliar material.

title: Dachshund Enrichment: Keep It at Floor Level
seoTitle: Dachshund Enrichment Guide
excerpt: A dachshund is a scent hound with a spine that fails. That combination means the best enrichment for the breed is also the safest: nose down, four feet on the ground.
imageAlt: A dachshund digging into a sand pit with its nose buried, tail up
author: Mike

faqs.q: Why does enrichment for a dachshund need special care?
faqs.a: Because of the spine. Dachshunds are the breed most associated with intervertebral disc disease, and a great many activities other dogs do freely, jumping off sofas, stairs, hard landings, carry real risk here.

faqs.q: What can they do safely?
faqs.a: Almost anything at floor level. Digging, scent work, puzzle feeding and tracking all give a dachshund a genuine job with four feet on the ground, and they happen to be exactly what the breed was designed for.

faqs.q: Is there evidence that scent work helps dogs?
faqs.a: Yes. Dogs given nosework approached an ambiguous bowl significantly faster afterwards on a cognitive bias test, the standard optimism measure, while dogs given heelwork did not change. For a scent-hunting breed that cannot jump, it is close to ideal.

faqs.q: Should I stop my dachshund using stairs?
faqs.a: Manage them rather than relying on the dog to be sensible. Ramps onto furniture, carrying up and down stairs or gating them off, and supporting the whole body when lifting are the standard recommendations.

faqs.q: Does weight affect the back?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is one of the few risk factors an owner fully controls. Extra weight increases load on a spine that is already the breed's weak point, so weight control is spinal care rather than a cosmetic concern.

faqs.q: Why is my dachshund digging up the garden?
faqs.a: Because it was bred to go underground after badgers. Digging is the breed doing its actual job, and a dedicated digging pit turns a destructive habit into the single best enrichment available for the breed.

title: How Much Does Degu Ownership Really Cost?
seoTitle: Degu Price: $10 to $50, Plus $375 to $520 Setup
excerpt: Degus are affordable individually, and the budgeting point with this species is that 'individually' isn't how you should be thinking about the purchase at all.
imageAlt: Two degus sitting together beside a small stack of coins
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a degu itself cost?
faqs.a: $10 to $50 each, whether from a breeder, pet store, or rescue, with adoption fees often landing at the lower end. Because degus are obligately social, budget for at least a same-sex pair from the start rather than one animal.

faqs.q: What does a full degu setup cost upfront?
faqs.a: Roughly $375 to $520 of equipment to house a pair properly, before the animals. Most of that is the large multi-level cage, with a solid exercise wheel, bedding, hides, and a sand bath setup behind it.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing monthly costs for a pair of degus?
faqs.a: Modest, and comparable to other small rodents. Hay, low-sugar pellets, and bedding make up most of it. Sugary treats and fruit are off the table for this species, which keeps the diet budget simpler rather than more expensive.

faqs.q: How much does degu vet care cost?
faqs.a: You'll want an exotics-experienced vet. Dental work for overgrown teeth and diabetes management are the two most likely reasons for a visit, common enough in this species to budget for proactively rather than treat as a remote possibility.

faqs.q: How long do degus live, and how does that affect the cost math?
faqs.a: 5 to 8 years in captivity, against a wild animal that seldom passes 2 years. That's longer than many small rodents, the hamster included, so treat a pair as a multi-year commitment.

title: Degu Enrichment: The Dust Bath Is a Message Board
seoTitle: Degu Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Degus dust bathe more on sand a familiar animal has already used. It is scent marking as much as grooming, which changes how you should offer it.
imageAlt: Two degus rolling in a shallow sand bath inside a tall multi-level cage
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there research on degu behavior?
faqs.a: Yes, and more than most exotic pets, because degus are used as a research model for diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. The behavioral work most useful to a keeper is on dust bathing, which turns out to be social communication as well as coat care.

faqs.q: What did the dust bathing research find?
faqs.a: Degus dust bathe at a higher rate on soil previously used by a familiar animal, and dust bathing is involved in communication during male-to-male interactions specifically. In wild colonies the bathing sites are marked with urine and anal gland secretions.

faqs.q: Does that change how I should offer a sand bath?
faqs.a: It argues for offering it to the group rather than to one animal in isolation, and for not sterilizing every trace between sessions when the same animals share it. It also means some soiling of the sand is the point rather than a failure.

faqs.q: Can degus be kept alone?
faqs.a: No. They are colonial and highly social, and at least two should be kept together. Isolated degus are reported to become aggressive or to self-mutilate, and a solitary degu is a welfare problem rather than a simpler setup.

faqs.q: Are degus nocturnal?
faqs.a: No, and this is one of the better things about them as pets. Degus are diurnal, so they are awake when you are, which makes the enrichment you provide something you will see used.

faqs.q: Why does the diet matter so much for a degu?
faqs.a: They are extremely prone to diabetes and cannot process sugar properly, including fruit and many commercial treats. That constrains food-based enrichment more than for any other pet rodent, so foraging has to be built on safe, low-sugar material.

title: Degu Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and Why They Stop Eating
seoTitle: What Do Degus Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: Degu feeding comes down to one rule that matters more than anything else: sugar is dangerous for this species, not just something to limit.
imageAlt: Degu eating timothy hay next to a small dish of sugar-free pellets
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What should a degu's diet be built around?
faqs.a: Grass hay, unlimited: timothy, meadow, or orchard. On top of it, a small measured daily amount of pellet made for degus or chinchillas, with no molasses, sugar, dried fruit, seeds, or colorful pieces in it. Guinea pig pellet, or half guinea pig and half chinchilla, is an acceptable substitute.

faqs.q: How much should I feed my degu?
faqs.a: Hay around the clock, no limit, that's the foundation. Pellets get measured instead: roughly 1 to 2 tablespoons per degu a day. Given free access to both, a degu picks the calorie-dense pellets over hay and ends up short on fiber.

faqs.q: Why is sugar so dangerous for degus specifically?
faqs.a: Insulin activity in this rodent is unusually low, which is why degus are studied as a natural model for diabetes: even modest added sugar brings the disease on readily. So fruit, honey, molasses, and sugary treats get avoided almost entirely, not moderated the way treats are for other small pets.

faqs.q: Do degus need vitamin C supplements like guinea pigs do?
faqs.a: No. They make their own vitamin C internally, which guinea pigs can't, so there's nothing to source. On a correct hay-and-pellet diet they generally need no added vitamins or minerals at all.

faqs.q: What foods should I never feed a degu?
faqs.a: Past fruit and sugar: starchy vegetables such as corn, peas, and potatoes, seeds and nuts as regular fare, and rabbit food, which can contain an ingredient toxic to degus. Hamster and gerbil mixes are the wrong fit as well, too much protein and seed for this species.

faqs.q: Why has my degu stopped eating?
faqs.a: Dental problems (sharp tooth spurs that cut the mouth), mouth ulcers, digestive bloating from too rich or too rapidly changed a diet, infection, and dehydration are all documented causes. Diabetes itself can also suppress appetite. Degus tend to hide illness until it's fairly advanced, so don't wait out a persistent refusal.

title: Two Pets Where You're Really Buying a Pair
seoTitle: Degu vs Gerbil: Which Small Pet Fits You? Key Differences
excerpt: The hamster is a lesson in solitude, one per cage, always. Degus and gerbils teach the exact opposite lesson, and it's worth understanding before you bring just one home.
imageAlt: Side by side of a pair of degus on a climbing platform and a pair of gerbils digging in deep bedding
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Can you keep just one degu or one gerbil?
faqs.a: No, not well. Both species are obligately social, and a solitary animal of either kind becomes stressed rather than simply lonely. Plan for a same-sex pair or small group from the start.

faqs.q: What's the one health risk specific to degus that gerbils don't share?
faqs.a: Diabetes. Degus have a genuine genetic predisposition toward it, and even small amounts of fruit or sugary treats can trigger the disease, a far stricter dietary rule than most small pets need.

faqs.q: Do degus and gerbils need the same kind of enclosure?
faqs.a: No. Degus need height and climbing room in a tall, solid-floored cage. Gerbils need genuine digging depth, 6 to 10 inches or more, in a glass tank a wire cage simply can't hold.

title: How to Handle a Degu (And Why It Needs a Friend)
seoTitle: How to Handle a Degu Safely
excerpt: Degus are curious, intelligent, social animals, and two facts about this species stand in direct contrast to the hamster, worth understanding clearly before you bring one home.
imageAlt: Person letting a degu climb onto their open hand
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Can I keep just one degu?
faqs.a: No. Degus are highly social and need to live in same-sex pairs or small groups. A solitary degu becomes stressed, which shows up as neurotic or aggressive behavior over time, the direct opposite of the solitary Syrian hamster, which must be housed alone.

faqs.q: Are degus active during the day or at night?
faqs.a: During the day. Degus are diurnal, so yours is awake and up for interaction on roughly your own schedule. Anyone coming from a nocturnal hamster will notice the difference immediately.

faqs.q: Can you pick a degu up by the tail?
faqs.a: Never. Grasping pressure on the tail causes tail slip, where the skin and fur come away. It doesn't grow back and it needs a vet. Scoop by the body.

faqs.q: Are degus easy to tame?
faqs.a: Yes, with regular, gentle handling. They're naturally curious and vocal, chirping and squeaking as part of normal communication, and tend to tame well compared to more skittish small rodents.

title: Common Degu Health Issues (Diabetes Is the One to Really Understand)
seoTitle: Degu Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Degus carry one health risk that's unusual among small pets, and understanding it should shape your entire approach to feeding this species from day one.
imageAlt: Degu being examined by an exotic veterinarian
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Why are degus so prone to diabetes?
faqs.a: They're naturally insulin-resistant, with a genetic predisposition toward diabetes that most small mammals don't share. Even small amounts of fruit, carrot, peas, corn, or sugary treats can trigger the disease, and veterinary literature flags the species as one where that predisposition creates real, ongoing management challenges.

faqs.q: What are the signs of diabetes in a degu?
faqs.a: Increased drinking and urination, weight changes, cloudy eyes from cataracts, thinning coat, and lethargy. Once diabetes develops it can be managed but not cured, so prevention through a strict sugar-free, fruit-free diet matters far more than with most pets.

faqs.q: What's the most common reason degus see a vet?
faqs.a: Dental disease. Molar malocclusion is the most frequently diagnosed dental disorder in degus, and the signs are drooling or a wet chin, dropped food, weight loss, and watery eyes. Healthy teeth look orange, not white.

faqs.q: What causes bumblefoot in degus?
faqs.a: Standing on wire flooring, which causes red, swollen, or scabbed footpads. It's manageable at home early by switching to solid flooring, but an infected case needs a vet.

faqs.q: How hot is too hot for a degu?
faqs.a: Above about 77°F. Degus tolerate heat poorly and should stay below that, out of direct sun. Heatstroke here is an emergency.

title: Is It Legal to Own a Degu? State-by-State Guide
seoTitle: Are Degus Legal? Banned in 8 of 52 Jurisdictions
excerpt: The degu is the most restricted small rodent kept as a pet in the US, and the reason repeats almost word for word from state to state: the cleared-rodent list names the chinchilla, guinea pig, gerbil, hamster, mouse and rat, and stops there.
imageAlt: Degu sitting on a wooden ledge holding forage in its forepaws
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Where are degus illegal?
faqs.a: Eight jurisdictions bar them outright: California, Colorado, Alaska, Connecticut, Georgia, New Mexico, Hawaii and the District of Columbia. Seven more require a permit, including Florida, Idaho, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Nevada and New Jersey. That leaves 34 where a degu is simply legal.

faqs.q: Why is the degu restricted when chinchillas and guinea pigs are not?
faqs.a: Because most of these rules work from a list of cleared rodents rather than a list of banned ones. Alaska, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Connecticut all name the chinchilla, guinea pig, gerbil, hamster, mouse and rat, and the degu is absent from every one of them. In Arkansas the omission looks deliberate rather than accidental, since its close relatives are all listed.

faqs.q: Is a captive-bred degu treated differently?
faqs.a: Rarely. The District of Columbia limits its rodent exception to domesticated species, and a degu is a wild species bred in captivity rather than a domesticated one, which puts it outside. Alabama's rule turns on the undefined phrase wild rodent and has the same problem: captive breeding does not create a domesticated lineage.

faqs.q: What does an unclear status mean here?
faqs.a: That the rule could reach the animal but never says so. Alabama and Pennsylvania both fall here. Pennsylvania names the degu nowhere, and what arguably catches it is a catch-all about wildlife captive bred in another state. Treat unclear as a reason to ask the state directly, not as permission.

title: Degu Enclosure Setup: Tall, Solid, and Genuinely Cool
seoTitle: Degu Enclosure Setup Guide
excerpt: A degu enclosure needs to support an active, social, day-active pair, tall, solid-floored, and cool enough to keep this heat-sensitive species comfortable.
imageAlt: Tall multi-level degu enclosure with ramps, a solid wheel, and a wooden nest box
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size enclosure does a degu pair need?
faqs.a: 24 by 18 by 24 inches for a pair at minimum, and larger is always better. Go tall and multi-level, with ramps and platforms, since this is a climbing species.

faqs.q: What temperature should a degu's room be?
faqs.a: 65 to 70°F, cool by small-pet standards. Heat is poorly tolerated, so keep the cage off windows, radiators, and direct sun, and never let the room climb toward 77°F.

faqs.q: Does a degu need sand or dust for bathing?
faqs.a: A sand or dust bath two to three times a week supports healthy coat condition and is a real physiological need, not optional grooming. Bathing sand is generally the gentler, better-suited choice for degus specifically, finer chinchilla dust is a reasonable alternative but was formulated for chinchilla fur.

faqs.q: Can a degu use a hamster wheel?
faqs.a: No, a hamster wheel is far too small. Use a solid wheel of 11 to 12 inches: wire or mesh catches toes and tails and causes real injury.

faqs.q: What bedding is safe for a degu?
faqs.a: Dust-free aspen shavings or a paper bedding, with plenty of hay and a deep area to dig in. No cedar, and nothing dusty or sugary.

title: Degu vs. Chinchilla: Which Long-Lived Rodent Fits Your Schedule
seoTitle: Degu vs. Chinchilla: Full Comparison
excerpt: Degu or chinchilla? The differences in daytime versus nighttime activity, sugar sensitivity, and just how much longer one of them lives, not just which one looks softer.
imageAlt: A degu and a chinchilla side by side for comparison
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Is a degu or a chinchilla awake during the day?
faqs.a: A degu, in most cases. Degus are unusual among pet rodents for being diurnal, most active from morning through early evening, which means an owner is likely to see one out and active. Chinchillas are nocturnal to crepuscular, spending most of the day asleep and becoming active in the evening and overnight.

faqs.q: Can degus eat the same treats as chinchillas?
faqs.a: No, and this matters more than it sounds. Degus have a genetic intolerance to sugar and are highly prone to diabetes, so fruit, honey, and other sugary treats that are an occasional fine indulgence for many small pets need to be avoided almost entirely. Chinchillas don't share that same acute sugar sensitivity, though both species still do best on a hay-heavy, low-sugar diet overall.

faqs.q: Do degus and chinchillas both need dust baths?
faqs.a: Yes, this is one of the genuine similarities between the two. Both species have fur too dense to dry properly if it gets wet with water, so both need regular access to volcanic dust for bathing rather than a water bath.

faqs.q: Which lives longer, a degu or a chinchilla?
faqs.a: Chinchillas, by a wide margin. A degu typically gets 5 to 8 years in captivity and a chinchilla 10 to 20, roughly double, which makes the chinchilla one of the longest-lived rodents in the pet trade.

faqs.q: Which is more social, a degu or a chinchilla?
faqs.a: Degus have the more clearly documented need for company: they're colonial in the wild and are best kept in pairs, with isolated degus at real risk of loneliness, depression, and self-harming behaviors like overgrooming. Chinchillas can also benefit from a companion, but the welfare stakes of housing one alone are less severe than they are for a degu.

title: How Much Does Discus Ownership Really Cost?
seoTitle: Discus Fish Price: $20 to $450, Plus $600 to $800 Setup
excerpt: Discus are one of the pricier community fish you can keep, and the cost isn't the fish itself, it's the filtration and water-change routine this species demands.
imageAlt: Discus fish swimming in a tall, well-filtered planted aquarium
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a discus fish cost?
faqs.a: $20 to $40 for young, common strains, more typically $50 to $150 for nicer adult specimens, and $200 to $450 or more for premium and rare strains like blue diamond or pigeon blood. Since discus need a group of 5 to 6 or more to feel secure, budget for that multiplier rather than a single fish's price tag.

faqs.q: What does a proper discus tank setup cost?
faqs.a: Roughly $600 to $800 for a real 55-gallon setup, tank, strong filtration, heater, substrate, driftwood, and plants, and more once you add an RO/DI unit for hard tap water or step up to a 75-gallon-plus tank.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing monthly costs for a discus?
faqs.a: Roughly $20 to $50 a month in food, quality pellets or granules, frozen bloodworms and brine shrimp, sometimes a beef-heart mix, plus water conditioner and test kit supplies. The bigger recurring cost is the electricity and water behind the frequent, large water changes this species needs to stay healthy.

faqs.q: Do discus need regular vet visits?
faqs.a: Rarely. Aquatic vet care is uncommon and specialized, and most keepers manage illness themselves with water-quality correction and over-the-counter medications like metronidazole. Budget for medication and a water test kit on hand rather than office visits.

faqs.q: How long do discus live?
faqs.a: The commonly cited range is 10 to 15 years with excellent, stable care, though some sources put the typical captive lifespan nearer 8 to 10. Consistency counts for more here than with most community fish: clean, stable water all year tends to buy meaningfully longer life than water that is good one week and neglected the next.

title: Discus Enrichment: A Nervous Cichlid Needs a Group and a Quiet Room
seoTitle: Discus Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Discus are shy cichlids that hold a pecking order. In small groups the bottom fish has nowhere to be, which is why six is the number people give.
imageAlt: A group of discus hanging together among tall plant stems and vertical driftwood
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there research on discus welfare?
faqs.a: Not on the species directly. The nearest evidence is the 2010 home aquarium group size study, which found the effect of group size on welfare was species-specific and, notably, found no group size effect for angelfish, the other large cichlid in the study.

faqs.q: Does that mean group size does not matter for discus?
faqs.a: No, and the reason is the hierarchy rather than shoaling. Discus establish a pecking order, and in a group of three or four the lowest-ranked fish is singled out with nowhere to go. Six or more spreads it, which is why that number is the standard advice.

faqs.q: What is the hardest part of keeping discus?
faqs.a: Water. They want warm, soft, very clean and above all stable conditions, and they react badly to swings that other cichlids shrug off. Most discus problems are water problems that started weeks earlier.

faqs.q: Do they need a tall tank?
faqs.a: Yes. Like angelfish they are laterally compressed and deep-bodied, so vertical space is the constrained dimension. A tall tank of the same volume is worth considerably more to them than a long shallow one.

faqs.q: Why are my discus always hiding?
faqs.a: Often the tank's position. Discus are nervous fish and a tank in a high-traffic spot, or one with people looming over it, produces animals that spend their time at the back. Location is an enrichment decision for this species.

faqs.q: Can discus be kept in a community tank?
faqs.a: With care and with the right tank mates. The warm temperatures they need rule out many common community fish, and boisterous or nippy species stress them badly. A species tank is the simplest answer.

title: Discus Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and the Beef-Heart Debate
seoTitle: What Do Discus Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: Discus have unusually small mouths for such a broad-bodied fish, and their fry start life feeding on a parent's own skin, two details that shape almost everything about how this species eats.
imageAlt: Discus fish feeding on frozen bloodworms near the middle of the water column
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How often should I feed my discus?
faqs.a: Adults 2 to 3 times a day, in small amounts they clear within a few minutes, rather than one large daily meal. Discus have a short gut for their body size, and smaller, more frequent meals suit that digestive setup better than a single big feeding.

faqs.q: What should the bulk of a discus diet be?
faqs.a: A quality discus-formulated pellet or granule, sized appropriately for this species' small mouth, supplemented regularly with frozen or live bloodworms and brine shrimp. Many experienced keepers also feed a beef-heart mix as part of the rotation, though it works better as a supplement than as the sole staple.

faqs.q: Is beef heart good for discus?
faqs.a: In moderation, yes, it's lean, high in protein, and easily digestible, and a controlled feeding study found no growth penalty when beef heart was blended with shrimp meat rather than fed alone. Fed as the only food, though, its fat content and poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio are real concerns, so most sources recommend trimming visible fat and treating it as part of a rotation rather than a daily staple.

faqs.q: How do newly hatched discus fry feed?
faqs.a: On mucus secreted from both parents' skin, a genuine, scientifically documented form of parental care called biparental mucus feeding, not hobbyist folklore. Fry feed on it most heavily for roughly the first two weeks after becoming free-swimming, with a gradual weaning process over the following two weeks as parents start swimming away more often.

faqs.q: Why has my discus stopped eating?
faqs.a: New-tank stress is the most common normal cause, expect some hesitation for the first few days after a move or a new introduction. Poor or fluctuating water quality, a disturbed or high-traffic tank location, and internal parasites are the other common explanations, and a discus that's hiding as well as refusing food points more toward stress or water quality than pickiness.

faqs.q: What food size mistake do new discus keepers make most often?
faqs.a: Feeding food sized for a typical community fish or a large cichlid. Discus mouths are noticeably small for how broad-bodied the fish is, and food that's too large gets ignored or spat back out rather than eaten, which can look like a health problem when it's just a sizing mismatch.

title: Discus Aren't Handled, But They Are Surprisingly Social for a Cichlid
seoTitle: Discus Behavior: Social Life & Stress Triggers
excerpt: Discus aren't a hands-on pet, but there's an important behavioral fact to understand before stocking a tank with them: unlike most cichlids, which pair off and defend territory, this one wants company.
imageAlt: A group of discus fish schooling together in a planted aquarium
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Do discus need to be kept in groups?
faqs.a: Yes. Unlike most cichlids, which pair off and defend territory, discus are a schooling fish that develop a social hierarchy within the group and become noticeably more stressed and reclusive when kept alone or in a pair outside of active breeding. Most sources recommend at least 5 to 6 individuals.

faqs.q: Why is my discus hiding?
faqs.a: Stress, most likely. Sudden movement, loud noise, bright light, and a busy spot in the house all set this species off. A new arrival that hides for a few days or even a few weeks is settling in, not necessarily ill.

faqs.q: How should I acclimate a new discus?
faqs.a: Carefully and without rushing, but sources disagree on the specific method. General fishkeeping guidance often recommends a slow drip acclimation for sensitive species, while some discus-specialty breeders argue drip acclimation can be more stressful for discus specifically, since it prolongs the fish's time in a small, oxygen-depleted bag while temperature slowly equalizes. Either way, keep the lights off for several hours after introduction and don't feed immediately.

faqs.q: Can I tell a male discus from a female?
faqs.a: Only with real difficulty outside of breeding. A more pointed dorsal fin and slightly larger body size are rough visual indicators used by some keepers, but they're not fully reliable. The only truly certain method is the genital papilla, which becomes visible during spawning, pointed on males and rounder and blunter on females, and even that structure retracts and is hard to see outside of that window.

faqs.q: Can discus live with neon tetras?
faqs.a: Not well, long term, and this one is debated. Discus need sustained 82 to 86°F water, and several dedicated discus care guides either specifically recommend against neon tetras or simply don't list them as compatible, favoring cardinal tetras instead, though at least one general fish-store care guide does list neons as compatible. Cardinal tetras tolerate the warmth more reliably and are the safer, more commonly recommended choice.

title: Common Discus Health Issues (And What Actually Prevents Them)
seoTitle: Discus Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Discus have a real reputation for being delicate, and most of what backs that up traces to water quality and stress, just with a narrower margin for error than most fish.
imageAlt: Discus fish in a clean, well-filtered tank showing healthy fins and coloring
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What causes most discus health problems?
faqs.a: Water quality and stress, the same pattern behind most fish health issues, just with less margin for error. Discus are more sensitive to ammonia, nitrite, and unstable conditions than a lot of hardier community fish, which is why this isn't a species for an uncycled or newly established tank.

faqs.q: What is hole-in-the-head disease in discus?
faqs.a: A condition causing pitting, erosion, and small holes around the head and lateral line, historically linked to the parasite Hexamita or the closely related Spironucleus, along with poor water quality, stress, and nutritional gaps. Treatment centers on metronidazole alongside correcting water conditions, and catching it early matters, advanced cases can be disfiguring.

faqs.q: Does diet cause hole-in-the-head disease?
faqs.a: It's less settled than hobbyist folklore suggests. A controlled 2019 study in the Journal of Fish Diseases fed discus a severely calcium-deficient diet for 16 weeks and found it did not produce hole-in-the-head lesions or bone loss, which pushes back on the common claim that a poor diet alone is the direct cause. Water quality and stress remain the better-supported explanations.

faqs.q: How do you treat ich in discus?
faqs.a: Quarantine and raise the temperature, though discus-specific sources go higher than the standard advice for other fish, up to around 90°F rather than 86°F, since discus already live near the upper end of ich's tolerance range. Daily water changes and a copper or formalin-based treatment during quarantine round out the protocol.

faqs.q: What are flukes, and are they a real risk for discus?
faqs.a: Yes, more so than for a lot of community fish. Gill and skin flukes are parasitic flatworms causing labored breathing, flashing against decor, and excess mucus production, treated with praziquantel or a dedicated fluke medication. Left untreated, gill flukes in particular can cause real breathing distress.

title: Discus Tank Setup: Why the Water-Change Routine Matters More Than the Gallon Number
seoTitle: Discus Tank Setup Guide
excerpt: Discus tolerate a narrower range of water conditions than most community fish, and the tank size number matters less than most people expect, the water-change routine is what separates a discus tank that works from one that doesn't.
imageAlt: Tall discus aquarium with driftwood, broadleaf plants, and visible filtration equipment
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size tank does a discus need?
faqs.a: 55 gallons is commonly cited as the practical minimum for a small group, though several experienced sources push that to 75 gallons or more, since a 55-gallon tank forces noticeably more frequent water changes to keep pace with this species' bioload. Taller tanks are preferred over long, low ones given this fish's body shape.

faqs.q: What temperature do discus need?
faqs.a: 82 to 86°F, warmer than nearly every other common community fish, warm enough that it narrows the tankmate list. Wild Heckel discus take water closer to 90°F, but 82 to 86°F is the standard target for captive-bred fish.

faqs.q: What water chemistry do discus need?
faqs.a: Soft and slightly acidic, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0. That mirrors the Amazon blackwater the species comes from, where wild pH runs 6.0 to 6.5 and can drop as low as 4. Hard tap water usually needs an RO or RO/DI unit to get there.

faqs.q: What filtration is best for a discus tank?
faqs.a: Debated. Canister filters are the most common modern choice and handle this species' heavy bioload well, but at least one discus-specialty source argues against them as sealed systems that compete with the fish for dissolved oxygen, recommending a hang-on-back or wet-dry filter instead, or a canister paired with extra aeration. Sponge filters are the standard choice for fry and breeding tanks.

faqs.q: How often do discus tanks need water changes?
faqs.a: More often than most community tanks, weekly changes in the 25 to 50% range are commonly recommended, and some serious keepers change water every 2 to 3 days. This is the single biggest recurring task with this species and matters more to long-term health than almost any other setup choice.

title: Do Dolphins Have Names? What the Research Actually Shows
seoTitle: Do Dolphins Have Names? The Real Science
excerpt: Bottlenose dolphins really do use something like names for each other. The research behind that claim is narrower, and more interesting, than the headline.
imageAlt: A bottlenose dolphin swimming just below the surface in clear blue water, photographed from the side in daylight
author: Michael Ryan
myth: Dolphins call each other by name.
truth: Each one invents a signature whistle and answers to it. Calling that a name overstates a narrower and stranger finding.

title: Bloat in Dogs: The Emergency Every Large-Breed Owner Should Know
seoTitle: Dog Bloat (GDV): Warning Signs to Know
excerpt: Bloat can kill a healthy dog within hours - the early signs, which breeds are most at risk, and why this is always a drive-to-the-vet-now emergency.
imageAlt: Large deep-chested dog resting calmly indoors after a meal
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What's the difference between bloat and GDV?
faqs.a: Bloat on its own just means the stomach has filled with gas, food, or fluid and distended - uncomfortable, but not always immediately fatal. GDV (gastric dilatation-volvulus) is what happens when that distended stomach also twists on itself, cutting off its own blood supply along with the spleen. Plain bloat can progress into GDV within hours, which is why both are treated as emergencies rather than waiting to see which one it is.

faqs.q: Which breeds are most at risk?
faqs.a: Deep-chested large and giant breeds top the list: Great Danes, Standard Poodles, German Shepherds, Weimaraners, Saint Bernards, and Doberman Pinschers among them. Labradors and other moderately deep-chested large breeds carry some risk too, just less than the extreme cases. Chest depth relative to width matters more than raw body size.

faqs.q: Does raising food bowls prevent bloat?
faqs.a: No, and this is one of the more persistent pieces of outdated advice still floating around. A widely cited Purdue University study actually found elevated bowls associated with higher bloat risk in at-risk breeds, not lower. Feeding from a normal, floor-level bowl is the current recommendation.

faqs.q: Can bloat happen without a big meal?
faqs.a: Yes. Stress, eating too fast, and exercising right after a meal all play a role independent of how much food was actually eaten, and genetics matters too - dogs with a first-degree relative that bloated are at higher risk regardless of feeding habits.

faqs.q: Is preventive gastropexy surgery worth it for high-risk breeds?
faqs.a: For many high-risk breeds, yes - vets often recommend it, sometimes performed at the same time as a spay or neuter to avoid a second anesthesia event. A gastropexy doesn't stop the stomach from filling with gas, but it tacks the stomach to the abdominal wall so it can't twist, which is the part that actually kills. That single change dramatically lowers the odds of a fatal outcome.

title: Dog Enrichment: Let Them Sniff, and the Dog Gets More Optimistic
seoTitle: Dog Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Two weeks of nosework made dogs measurably more optimistic on a cognitive bias test. The control group did heelwork and did not change.
imageAlt: A dog nose-down working a scent trail through long grass
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there research showing dog enrichment works?
faqs.a: Yes, and one study is unusually clean. Duranton and Horowitz gave twenty pet dogs either nosework or heelwork, then tested them on a cognitive bias task.
