faqs.q: What is scale rot and what causes it in hognose snakes?
faqs.a: Also called blister disease. Damp, dirty substrate causes it, and the sign is discolored or blistered belly scales. Keeping the substrate dry and clean prevents it, which is what this species wants anyway. See a vet if it moves past mild discoloration.

faqs.q: Do hognose snakes get mites or internal parasites?
faqs.a: Both happen, and both are treatable. Run periodic fecal checks, especially on a newly acquired snake, to catch parasites early.

title: Is It Legal to Own a Hognose Snake? State-by-State Guide
seoTitle: Is a Hognose Snake Legal in Your State? Full Guide
excerpt: Hognose snakes are mildly rear-fanged, but that doesn't make them a regulated venomous species anywhere we checked. The restriction to watch for is Georgia, which bans keeping native hognose as pets regardless of captive-bred origin.
imageAlt: Hognose snake with its distinctive upturned snout
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Is a hognose snake venomous, and does that make it illegal?
faqs.a: Hognose snakes are mildly rear-fanged, meaning they produce a weak venom used mostly to subdue toads, but medical case reports describe bites as causing local swelling at worst, not a systemic reaction. Every state venomous-reptile law we checked, including Alabama, Kentucky, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Florida, specifically excludes the genus Heterodon by name.

faqs.q: Can I legally own a hognose snake in Georgia?
faqs.a: No. Georgia's native-wildlife law bans keeping Eastern and Southern hognose snakes as pets regardless of whether the animal is wild-caught or captive-bred, which is a real exception to the otherwise permissive pattern in most states.

faqs.q: What changed with Colorado's 2026 rule?
faqs.a: Colorado now allows captive-bred Western and Plains hognose snakes to be possessed, sold, and transported with documentation, effective May 1, 2026. Wild collection of any native Colorado hognose is now banned, and Eastern hognose is excluded from the new legalization entirely.

title: Western Hognose Snake Tank Setup: Dry, Deep, and Built for Burrowing
seoTitle: Hognose Snake Tank Setup Guide
excerpt: Western hognose care comes down to a fairly short list of priorities: keep it dry, keep the substrate deep enough to burrow in, and get the heat source right.
imageAlt: Western hognose snake enclosure with deep substrate, basking bulb, and hides
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size enclosure does a Western hognose snake need?
faqs.a: A useful rule of thumb is roughly one square foot of floor space per foot of snake length. Adult males need a 20-gallon-equivalent minimum (around 30x13x13 inches); females grow noticeably larger and need a 40-gallon-equivalent minimum (36x18x16 inches). A 2x2x2 foot PVC enclosure works well as an adult setup for either sex. Floor space matters more than height, this is a ground-dwelling, burrowing species, not a climber.

faqs.q: What temperature does a hognose snake enclosure need?
faqs.a: A basking area around 90 to 95°F on one end, a cool side at 70 to 75°F, and a night temperature around 75 to 78°F. The commonly recommended heat source is a low-wattage halogen basking bulb over the substrate on a thermostat or dimmer, rather than a heat mat or ceramic heat emitter as the primary source.

faqs.q: How humid should a hognose snake enclosure be?
faqs.a: 30 to 50% ambient, dry compared with most pet snakes. Rather than misting the whole enclosure, run one dedicated humid hide for shedding and add moisture only there.

faqs.q: What substrate should I use for a hognose snake?
faqs.a: 3 to 6 inches of loose, dry, diggable substrate, commonly about 70% soil-based substrate to 30% reptile-safe sand. This is a fossorial species that uses the depth, so keep it deep and keep it dry.

faqs.q: Does a hognose snake need UVB lighting?
faqs.a: It isn't strictly required by every source, but hognoses are active during the day, unlike many pet snakes, and a low-output linear T5 bulb spanning part of the enclosure is increasingly recommended for this diurnal species, alongside a normal 12-hour light and dark cycle.

title: Honey Badgers: The Toughest Little Troublemakers on the Planet
seoTitle: Honey Badger: The World's Most Fearless Animal
excerpt: The 2002 Guinness Book called it the world's most fearless animal. We checked which of the honey badger's famous claims actually hold up.
imageAlt: A honey badger foraging in the African savanna, showing its distinctive black and white markings
author: Michael Ryan
myth: The honey badger is officially the world most fearless animal, and nothing can touch it.
truth: That was a 2002 print edition of Guinness. Lions and leopards prey on them, and adult annual mortality runs at 34 percent.

title: How a Glass Frog Hides Its Own Blood, and Why That Should Kill It
seoTitle: How Glass Frogs Hide Their Blood to Turn Clear
excerpt: A sleeping glass frog packs about 89 percent of its red blood cells into its liver, which is what makes it clear. Blood that concentrated should clot. It does not, and nobody yet knows why.
imageAlt: A glass frog gripping a green stem, its translucent belly showing the internal organs through the skin
author: Michael Ryan
myth: A glass frog is see-through because there is nothing much inside it.
truth: It packs 89 percent of its red blood cells into its liver to sleep. Blood that concentrated should clot, and somehow does not.

title: How Dangerous Are Sharks, Really? What the Numbers Actually Say
seoTitle: How Dangerous Are Sharks? The Real Numbers
excerpt: There were 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025. In the same period, people killed roughly 80 million sharks. Here is what the data actually shows.
imageAlt: A blacktip reef shark swimming calmly through clear blue water, seen from the side in bright daylight
author: Michael Ryan
myth: Sharks are one of the more dangerous animals to humans.
truth: There were 65 unprovoked bites worldwide in 2025. Over the same period people killed roughly 80 million sharks.

title: Honeybees Vote on Where to Live, and the Losing Side Gets Head-Butted Into Silence
seoTitle: How Honeybee Swarms Choose a New Home
excerpt: A swarm hanging off a branch is running a decision process. Scouts campaign by dancing, rivals are silenced by a head-butt and a beep, and the result is usually the best cavity available.
imageAlt: A dense honeybee swarm cluster hanging from a tree branch, thousands of bees forming a teardrop mass
author: Michael Ryan

title: Three Pets That Are a Bigger Deal Than They Look
seoTitle: Green Iguana, Fire Skink & Quaker Parakeet Compared
excerpt: A cheap baby lizard. A small, colorful skink. A parakeet barely bigger than a lovebird. None of these three look like they come with real strings attached. All three do.
imageAlt: Green iguana, fire skink, and Quaker parakeet shown side by side
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Is a green iguana a good pet for a first-time reptile owner?
faqs.a: No, despite the cheap $20 to $100 hatchling price suggesting otherwise. Adult males reach 6 to 7 feet and up to 20 pounds, need a custom walk-in enclosure at minimum 10x5x6 feet, and an estimated 70% of captive green iguanas die within their first year from inadequate care. This is squarely an advanced-keeper species.

faqs.q: Is a fire skink handleable like a blue-tongued skink?
faqs.a: No, and this is the most common misconception about the species. Fire skinks are shy, fast, and fossorial, closer to a beautiful display animal than a handling pet, a real temperament difference from the docile blue-tongued skink despite both being skinks.

faqs.q: Is it legal to own a Quaker parakeet everywhere in the US?
faqs.a: No. Quaker parakeets are banned or restricted in a meaningful number of US states over invasive-species concerns, since escaped birds build large stick nests on power infrastructure and form feral colonies. Check your state's wildlife or agriculture agency before buying, not after.

title: The Immortal Jellyfish Is Real, But It Does Not Live Forever
seoTitle: The Immortal Jellyfish: What It Actually Does
excerpt: Turritopsis dohrnii really can reverse its life cycle and turn back into a polyp. What it cannot do is survive being eaten, and most of them are.
imageAlt: A tiny transparent Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish with a bright red stomach and fine trailing tentacles, photographed against dark water
author: Michael Ryan
myth: The immortal jellyfish lives forever.
truth: It can reverse its life cycle back to a polyp, which is not the same as not dying. Most get eaten long before they get the chance.

title: Inherited Eye Disease: What Screening Actually Catches
seoTitle: Inherited Eye Disease in Dogs and Cats Explained
excerpt: Progressive retinal atrophy is not one disease. It is a family of them, caused by different broken genes in different breeds, which is why a PRA-clear result names one variant and says nothing about the rest.
imageAlt: Veterinary ophthalmologist examining a dog's eye with a slit lamp
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: My dog's PRA test came back clear. Is it safe from going blind?
faqs.a: From that one variant, yes. From progressive retinal atrophy, not necessarily. PRA is a family of diseases caused by different broken genes in different breeds, and over 20 separate PRA-causing mutations have been identified in dogs. A test names the variant it looks for and says nothing about the others. Golden Retrievers alone have three separate PRA genes with three separate tests. A clear result on one of them is exactly that.

faqs.q: What is the very first thing I would notice?
faqs.a: Usually behavior in the dark rather than anything you can see in the eye. A dog with early PRA becomes reluctant to go into dark rooms, hesitates going down stairs in poor light, and bumps into things at dusk while navigating the house perfectly at noon. Two other owner-noticed signs are pupils that look permanently large, and eyeshine that has got brighter, so the eyes glow more in photographs than they used to.

faqs.q: My old dog's eyes have gone cloudy blue. Is that a cataract?
faqs.a: Probably not. Nuclear sclerosis is a normal age change where the lens becomes denser, giving the pupil a hazy blue-grey look, and it does not cause blindness. A cataract is an actual opacity that blocks light. They look similar to an owner and completely different through an ophthalmoscope, so this is one where you genuinely cannot tell at home. The practical difference is that a dog with nuclear sclerosis still navigates normally.

faqs.q: The vet wants to reposition my dog's cherry eye rather than remove it. Why?
faqs.a: Because that pink lump is a working tear gland, not a growth. Sources put its contribution at somewhere between about a third and a half of the watery part of the tear film. Removing it substantially raises the risk of dry eye, which is painful, permanent and can itself impair vision. Repositioning tucks the gland into a pocket of tissue and secures it, with re-prolapse in roughly 5% to 20% of cases.

faqs.q: Does an eye certification mean my dog's eyes are healthy?
faqs.a: It means a board-certified ophthalmologist screened them and found nothing on that screen. The OFA is explicit that it is a screening exam and not a comprehensive ocular health examination, and it lists what is not routinely done: gonioscopy, tonometry, Schirmer tear test, electroretinography and ultrasonography. So goniodysgenesis, glaucoma, dry eye, early lens luxation and some early PRA can all be missed. The certificate is also valid for 12 months, not for life.

faqs.q: Are white cats really at higher risk of eye cancer?
faqs.a: White and unpigmented skin is the risk factor, and the sites it affects are exactly the ones around the eye: eyelids, nose, ear tips and lips. Prolonged ultraviolet exposure damages the DNA in those cells, producing solar keratosis first and squamous cell carcinoma after. Indoor cats are not exempt, because a favorite sunny windowsill delivers cumulative UV. Note that human sunscreen is unsafe for cats and must never be used near the eyes.

title: Invertebrate Emergency Plan: Power Outages, Travel, and Shipping
seoTitle: Invertebrate Emergency Plan: Outages, Travel, Shipping
excerpt: Power outages are mostly a non-event for a tarantula, and that's worth writing down plainly. The real risk in this corner of pet keeping is in a car, a shipping box, or a hermit crab's uniquely humidity-dependent setup.
imageAlt: A tarantula in a ventilated deli cup nestled inside a padded shipping box next to a battery hygrometer
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How long can a pet tarantula safely be left alone?
faqs.a: There's no single verified figure worth printing here, and most of what circulates online is hobbyist estimate rather than tested data. The more useful way to think about it is what actually runs out first. Tarantulas normally go without eating for stretches around a molt, described by the University of Illinois College of Veterinary Medicine as a completely normal physiologic fast, so missing the usual few-times-a-week feeding for several days rarely stresses a healthy adult. Water and stable humidity are the tighter constraint, so a full, shallow water dish and a securely sealed enclosure do more for a short trip than anything related to food.

faqs.q: Do I need a backup power plan for a pet tarantula, scorpion, or mantis during an outage?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most of these animals are kept at ordinary room temperature with no heat lamp or heat mat running day to day, so a power outage that doesn't also make the house dangerously cold changes very little for them. The animals worth actively worrying about during an outage are the minority kept on supplemental heat, and hermit crabs, which depend on both heat and humidity being actively maintained rather than merely comfortable.

faqs.q: Are hermit crabs different from tarantulas when it comes to power outages?
faqs.a: Yes, genuinely. A hermit crab is a crustacean, not an arachnid, and it breathes through modified gills that need consistently warm, humid air to function. That setup depends on active heating and moisture control in a way a room-temperature tarantula enclosure simply doesn't, which makes hermit crabs the clearest exception to the reassuring outage picture for this group of pets.

faqs.q: What's the safest way to transport a tarantula in a car?
faqs.a: Use a secure, ventilated, escape-proof container with soft substrate or paper towel to cushion any movement, and keep it upright and wedged so it can't tip, slide, or fall while the car is moving. Keep the container in the passenger area, never a trunk, and avoid temperature extremes, a hot closed car in summer or a freezing one in winter. A fall of even a modest height can rupture a tarantula's abdomen, which is the single biggest transport risk for this animal, not the ride itself.

faqs.q: Is it legal to ship a live tarantula or other invertebrate in the US?
faqs.a: Shipping live invertebrates is legal and happens routinely in the US, but the rules are genuinely carrier-specific and species-specific, and they change. USPS's own published mailing standards list spiders and poisonous insects as nonmailable, with a narrow exception for scorpions shipped for medical research or antivenin production, which is why most invertebrate shipments move through other carriers under separate live-animal programs instead. Federal plant-pest permitting and, for some crustaceans and mollusks, the Lacey Act's injurious wildlife list can also apply depending on the species. Always confirm current policy directly with the carrier and check applicable state and federal rules before shipping, don't rely on any single article, including this one, as the final word.

faqs.q: What's the most important thing to leave a pet sitter watching an invertebrate?
faqs.a: A short, specific do-not list matters more than a long one. Don't mist or feed beyond what's written down, don't open the enclosure unless it's on the list, and don't try to handle or move the animal. Invertebrate care mistakes are almost always the result of a well-meaning sitter improvising, not a lack of effort.

title: Invertebrate Molting 101: What's Normal, Species by Species
seoTitle: Invertebrate Molting 101: What's Normal
excerpt: How molting works in tarantulas, hermit crabs, jumping spiders, millipedes and stick insects - normal signs versus a failed molt, and why you should never disturb a molting pet.
imageAlt: Tarantula on natural substrate beside a freshly shed exoskeleton
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How do I know a molt failed versus is just taking a long time?
faqs.a: Duration alone isn't the tell - a hermit crab buried for three weeks is normal, while a tarantula visibly stuck half in and half out of its old exoskeleton for hours, with no progress, is not. Look for active struggling that isn't resolving, rather than just going by the clock.

faqs.q: Should I increase humidity before an expected molt?
faqs.a: Yes, for most species. Slightly elevated humidity during premolt helps the old exoskeleton separate cleanly from the new one underneath, which reduces the risk of a failed molt. Species-specific care guides typically note a premolt humidity bump for exactly this reason.

faqs.q: Can I speed up a molt that seems stalled?
faqs.a: No, and attempting to should be avoided entirely. Physically assisting a molt without experience or training frequently causes fatal injury, since the new exoskeleton underneath is extremely fragile. If a molt genuinely appears to have failed, an exotic vet or a highly experienced keeper is the only appropriate intervention.

faqs.q: Do invertebrates eat their old exoskeleton?
faqs.a: Many do, and it's normal, not a sign of a problem. The shed exoskeleton contains calcium and other nutrients, and species like tarantulas and some hermit crabs will consume all or part of it after a molt completes.

faqs.q: How long after a molt can I resume handling?
faqs.a: Wait until the new exoskeleton has visibly hardened, which is typically 7 to 14 days for a tarantula and often shorter for smaller species like jumping spiders. A freshly molted invertebrate is soft, fragile, and easily injured by even gentle handling.

title: Household Pesticides and Your Invertebrate Pet: The Hidden Hazard
seoTitle: Household Pesticides and Pet Invertebrate Safety
excerpt: A tarantula, scorpion, mantis, or millipede is an arthropod, and household insecticides are built to kill arthropods. Here's why a healthy spider can die overnight with no warning, and how to actually prevent it.
imageAlt: A tarantula enclosure sitting on a shelf away from an aerosol insect spray can and a plug-in insect repellent device on the other side of the room
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Can bug spray really kill a tarantula from across the room?
faqs.a: Yes, and this is the mechanism that catches most keepers off guard. Aerosol insecticides are usually pyrethroid-based, and the National Pesticide Information Center's general fact sheet on pyrethrins describes them as exciting the nervous system of insects that touch or eat them, leading quickly to paralysis and death. NPIC frames that for insects, and a tarantula is an arachnid rather than an insect, but both are arthropods sharing the same broad nervous system chemistry. A tarantula's book lungs pull air straight from the room, so drift from a spray used two rooms away, or fumes that settle onto a tank's mesh lid, can reach the animal without anyone spraying anywhere near the enclosure.

faqs.q: Is flea and tick treatment on my dog or cat dangerous to my tarantula or scorpion?
faqs.a: It can be, if the treated pet spends time in the same airspace or the product is a spray or powder rather than a fully absorbed spot-on. NPIC's fipronil fact sheet lists spot-on pet care products among the more than 50 registered fipronil formulations, and fipronil works by disrupting the central nervous system of the target pest. The safest practice is treating dogs and cats in a separate room from any invertebrate enclosure and letting the product dry fully before the animals share space again.

faqs.q: Are wild-caught feeder insects safe to feed a pet tarantula or mantis?
faqs.a: Not automatically. A 2021 Scientific Reports study by Brühl and colleagues found that flying insects collected in German nature conservation areas, protected land, not sprayed fields, were contaminated with an average of 16.7 different current-use pesticides per sample. That study did not test feeder insects specifically, but it shows wild insects outside actively treated land can still carry detectable residue, which is a real argument for sticking to commercially farmed feeders with no pesticide exposure history.

faqs.q: What do I do if I think my invertebrate has been exposed to a pesticide?
faqs.a: Move the animal and its enclosure to clean air immediately, away from the source, and open windows if the exposure happened indoors. There is no home antidote for pesticide toxicity in an invertebrate. Ventilating the space is the same first step the EPA gives for total release foggers, where the guidance is to leave doors and windows open to clear remaining fumes before anyone, including pets, returns. Beyond removing the animal from the contaminated air, there is little else a keeper can do at home, and there is no invertebrate-specific antidote or emergency vet protocol comparable to what exists for a dog or cat.

faqs.q: Do I need to tell a pest control company I keep invertebrates?
faqs.a: Yes, every time, and before any visit, not after. Ant, roach, and general perimeter treatments commonly use fipronil or pyrethroid products, per NPIC, and a technician has no way of knowing an enclosure of arthropods sits in a back bedroom unless you say so. Ask for the exact active ingredients being used, request that your invertebrate room be skipped or treated last with the door closed, and move enclosures to a separate closed room with the door sealed during and for several hours after any whole-house or building-wide treatment.

faqs.q: Which insecticide classes are most likely to be in my house right now?
faqs.a: Pyrethroids are by far the most common active ingredient in consumer aerosol sprays and foggers, built on the naturally derived pyrethrins found in chrysanthemum flowers, per NPIC. Neonicotinoids like imidacloprid show up in some ant and lawn products, and fipronil is common in ant bait stations, roach gel bait, and flea and tick spot-on treatments. All three target the nervous system, just at different receptor sites, which is why no single insecticide class is the safe one to reach for around an invertebrate pet.

title: Invertebrate Housekeeping: Quarantining a New Arrival, Cleaning the Enclosure, and Finding an Escapee
seoTitle: Invertebrate Quarantine, Cleaning and Escapes
excerpt: Three questions every new invertebrate keeper asks and no species page here answered: how long to isolate a new animal, how often to clean an enclosure that never looks dirty, and where a tarantula goes when the lid was left open.
imageAlt: A tarantula in a small clear quarantine enclosure with a water dish and paper towel substrate, set apart on a shelf from a row of larger planted enclosures
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How long should I quarantine a new invertebrate?
faqs.a: At least three months, in a different room from the rest of the collection if you have one, with its own tools. That is the tarantula hobby's figure and it covers the slow problems, mites and mold that build over weeks and the nematode infections that only show once the animal is established. A single first pet skips the room but not the watching.

faqs.q: How often do I clean an invertebrate enclosure?
faqs.a: Spot clean weekly: uneaten prey out within 24 hours, prey remains and droppings out as you see them, water dish rinsed and refilled. Replace the substrate every 6 to 12 months, or sooner if mold appears. A full strip-down is otherwise a disturbance the animal does not need, and a tarantula can sit on the same substrate for years.

faqs.q: My tarantula escaped. Where do I look?
faqs.a: Low, dark and warm, in the room it escaped from if it has been under two hours: under furniture, in dark corners, under the bed, in piles of clothes or shoes. Tree-dwellers climb instead, so check walls and bookshelves. Search at night with a flashlight, and put out a water dish or damp paper towel as bait, since an escapee goes looking for water first.

faqs.q: What do mites in the enclosure mean?
faqs.a: Usually that prey remains have been sitting too long in a damp, poorly ventilated enclosure. Most are harmless scavengers, and the fix is removing the remains and restoring ventilation. If they are on the animal itself, or on a fresh molt, a vet with invertebrate experience is the call rather than a chemical, since nearly every pesticide kills the pet along with the mites.

title: Rehousing an Invertebrate: Method, Timing, and Urticating Hair First Aid
seoTitle: Rehousing an Invertebrate: Method and First Aid
excerpt: Rehousing is two separate jobs, preparation and the catch-cup-and-card method itself, plus what to do if a New World tarantula flicks urticating hairs while it happens.
imageAlt: A tarantula being guided from an old enclosure into a new one using a clear catch cup and a piece of card, held low over a lined tub
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What is the catch cup and card method for rehousing a tarantula?
faqs.a: You lower a clear, smooth-sided cup over the animal, then slide a stiff piece of card or thin plastic underneath to seal it in, lifting cup and card together as one unit. The animal is never gripped or picked up by hand, and the whole transfer happens low over a lined tub in case the seal slips.

faqs.q: Can you rehouse a tarantula during a molt?
faqs.a: No. A tarantula in premolt, mid-molt, or freshly molted has a soft, still-hardening exoskeleton and soft fangs, and disturbing it during this window is one of the few genuinely absolute rules in invertebrate keeping. Wait until the new exoskeleton has visibly darkened and the animal is moving and gripping normally again.

faqs.q: What should you do if a tarantula or scorpion bolts during rehousing?
faqs.a: Mostly, nothing sudden. Stay still, let it run to a corner or under cover inside the tub you're already working in, and re-approach slowly with the cup once it settles. Grabbing at a bolting animal is how falls happen, and a fall is what actually injures a tarantula, not the bolt itself.

faqs.q: Which tarantulas have urticating hairs, and how are they used?
faqs.a: Urticating hairs are a New World tarantula trait specifically. Species from the Americas, including the commonly kept Chilean rose hair, can kick barbed hairs off the abdomen with their hind legs and flick them at a perceived threat. Old World species, like Poecilotheria and baboon spiders, never developed this defense and rely on a fast bite instead.

faqs.q: What's the first aid for tarantula urticating hairs in the skin, eyes, or airway?
faqs.a: For skin, press tape onto the area and lift it away to pull the barbed hairs out, which clinical sources describe as reducing the itching; repeat applications are often needed. For the eyes, stop touching it, shield it if you can, and get to an ophthalmologist or emergency care the same day rather than waiting. Any wheezing, throat tightness, or real difficulty breathing after an exposure is an emergency room visit, not a wait-and-see.

faqs.q: Do scorpions, mantises, and millipedes rehouse the same way as tarantulas?
faqs.a: No. A scorpion is moved with long tongs or a sealed transfer container because of the sting, not a fall risk. A mantis is cup-and-lid transferred gently because its legs and wings are fragile, not because it's fast to bolt. A millipede is slow enough to nudge with a soft brush, but it defends with a chemical secretion rather than hairs, so the handling risk and the first aid are both different.

title: IVDD: Why Short Legs and Bad Backs Come From the Same Gene
seoTitle: IVDD in Dogs: Grades, Genetics and Recovery Rates
excerpt: The retrogene that gives a Dachshund its short legs is the same one that wrecks its discs. It is not a side effect of the shape, it is the shape, and the odds ratio attached to it is 51.
imageAlt: Dachshund standing in profile showing the long back and short legs of a chondrodystrophic breed
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What does IVDD stand for?
faqs.a: Intervertebral disc disease. An intervertebral disc is the cushion between two vertebrae, with a gel-like core called the nucleus pulposus inside a tough fibrous ring called the annulus fibrosus. The discs let the spine bend and absorb shock. When one degenerates it can bulge or rupture into the spinal canal, and because the cord runs through a tunnel of bone there is nowhere for that material to go except into the cord.

faqs.q: How common is IVDD in Dachshunds?
faqs.a: Miniature Dachshunds have a lifetime prevalence of around 20%, against roughly 3.5% for dogs overall. A survey of 2,031 Dachshunds found 15.7% affected, and it varied by variety: Standard Smooth-Haired highest at 24.4%, Standard Wire-Haired lowest at 7.1%. The American College of Veterinary Surgeons estimates Dachshunds alone account for 40 to 75% of all IVDD cases.

faqs.q: What is the FGF4 retrogene?
faqs.a: An extra, reinserted copy of the fibroblast growth factor 4 gene. Dogs carry two, one on chromosome 18 and one on chromosome 12. The chromosome 12 copy produces both the short-legged build and premature disc degeneration, with an odds ratio of 51.23 for IVDD. It is semidominant for height but dominant for disc disease, so one copy is enough to carry the disc risk.

faqs.q: What is deep pain perception and why does everyone ask about it?
faqs.a: It is the deepest level of sensation in the limbs, tested by pinching the bone of a toe or the tail and watching for a real behavioral response such as a bark or turning the head. A reflex twitch of the leg does not count. In a paralyzed dog it is the single most important prognostic finding: with it intact, surgical recovery runs 85 to 95%, without it around 50%.

faqs.q: Do stairs and furniture cause IVDD?
faqs.a: The evidence does not support the usual advice. In a survey of 2,031 Dachshunds, dogs not allowed to jump on furniture had higher odds of IVDD, not lower, and dogs doing no stairs daily had higher odds than dogs doing a full flight. That is almost certainly reverse causation, owners restricting dogs after a diagnosis. What it does mean is that banning stairs has never been shown to prevent anything.

title: How Much Does a Jackson's Chameleon Really Cost?
seoTitle: Jackson's Chameleon Price: $50 to $250, Setup $400 to $525
excerpt: Jackson's chameleons sit in a comparable price range to the veiled chameleon, but the two species diverge in some important ways worth understanding before you buy.
imageAlt: Male Jackson's chameleon with three forward-facing horns perched on a branch
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a Jackson's chameleon cost to buy?
faqs.a: $90 to $150 typically, and prized, highly colored specimens of the primary subspecies reach $250. Wild-caught Hawaiian animals sometimes turn up cheaper, but Hawaii bars commercial export to the mainland, so a cheap Hawaiian animal was either exported before the rule or illegally, and it is frequently parasitized besides. Captive-bred is worth the higher price here.

faqs.q: What does the upfront enclosure setup cost?
faqs.a: Roughly $400 to $525, covering a tall screen or hybrid enclosure sized for an adult, a UVB fixture and bulb, a halogen basking bulb on a dimmer, a misting system, and live plants with moisture-retentive substrate.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing monthly costs?
faqs.a: Roughly $50 to $100 a month for feeder insects, supplements, live plants, and electricity for misting and lighting equipment, bringing annual costs to somewhere around $1,200 including occasional larger expenses.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for vet care?
faqs.a: Commonly $50 to $100 or more for a routine exam. Emergencies can run into the hundreds, gout, metabolic bone disease, and birth complications among them.

faqs.q: Do male and female Jackson's chameleons live the same length of time?
faqs.a: No. Males commonly live 8 to 10 years, while females typically live just 3 to 5 years, tied to the physical toll of giving birth to live young repeatedly rather than laying eggs.

faqs.q: Is a Jackson's chameleon more expensive to keep than a veiled chameleon?
faqs.a: Not meaningfully, both sit in a comparable price range. The differences between the two are biological rather than financial, Jackson's chameleons give live birth instead of laying eggs, and need a noticeably cooler setup thanks to their East African mountain origin.

title: Jackson's Chameleon Enrichment: A Mountain Animal in a Warm House
seoTitle: Jackson's Chameleon Enrichment Guide
excerpt: For this species the most valuable enrichment is a temperature most keepers are accidentally exceeding. Everything else comes after the enclosure stops being too hot.
imageAlt: A horned Jackson's chameleon moving along a mossy branch in a cool planted enclosure
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there enrichment research on Jackson's chameleons?
faqs.a: No. Nothing has been published on Trioceros jacksonii. The nearest evidence is the veiled chameleon isolation study, which found that hatchlings reared alone for two months grew into more submissive, duller, worse-foraging animals. Different genus, same family, so it is a reasonable borrow.

faqs.q: What makes Jackson's chameleons different from veiled chameleons?
faqs.a: Altitude. They come from cool, humid montane forest in East Africa, so they need noticeably lower temperatures and a real night-time drop. A room temperature that suits a veiled chameleon can be lethal to a Jackson's over time.

faqs.q: What is the most important enrichment item for this species?
faqs.a: Getting the temperature down. That sounds like husbandry rather than enrichment, and for a montane animal being kept too warm it is the change that unlocks every other behavior. A chronically overheated chameleon does not climb, hunt or display much of anything.

faqs.q: Do they need a misting system?
faqs.a: In practice, yes. They drink moving droplets off leaves, need high humidity with drying cycles between mistings, and the humidity requirement is higher than for most chameleons kept in the hobby. Hand spraying enough times a day is difficult to sustain.

faqs.q: Can Jackson's chameleons be kept together?
faqs.a: No, not as adults. They are less openly aggressive than veiled chameleons, which makes the stress harder to spot rather than absent. Solo housing is correct, and a subordinate chameleon in a shared enclosure declines quietly.

faqs.q: Are wild-caught Jackson's chameleons common?
faqs.a: Historically yes, and it matters here. Wild-caught animals arrive with parasite loads and transport stress, and a stressed imported chameleon needs quarantine, veterinary attention and quiet far more than it needs enrichment objects.

title: Jackson's Chameleon Feeding: Three Insects Every Other Day, and the Supplement That Causes Edema
seoTitle: What Do Jackson's Chameleons Eat? Feeding Schedule
excerpt: A Jackson's chameleon is the one lizard where more supplement is the common mistake. Here is the feeding schedule by age, the five-to-seven insect ceiling, the eye-width prey rule, the calcium and vitamin rhythm that keeps a montane chameleon out of edema and gout, and why it drinks before it eats.
imageAlt: A three-horned Jackson's chameleon on a branch with its tongue extended toward a cricket, water droplets on the leaves around it
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much should a Jackson's chameleon eat?
faqs.a: A baby eats as much as it will take. From six months to a year, about ten insects every other day. An adult, three well gut-loaded insects every other day, with five to seven per feeding as the ceiling. A pregnant female goes to five every other day, and more if she is still hunting. Every insect is no wider than the space between the chameleon's eyes.

faqs.q: How often do I dust with calcium and vitamins?
faqs.a: Lightly. The veterinary sheet dusts an adult's diet with plain calcium once a week and a multivitamin once a week. A growing juvenile under a year gets plain calcium more often, since that is when bones are being built. Either way the powder is D3-free, the vitamin product is low in vitamin A, and nothing goes on daily.

faqs.q: Why is oversupplementing dangerous for this species?
faqs.a: Jackson's chameleons are unusually sensitive to excess vitamin A and D. Too much shows as edema, fluid swelling at the throat and neck, and as gout. High-vitamin-D products can reach toxicity, and synthetic vitamin A is the ingredient most often behind the swelling. More powder is the common mistake here, not less.

faqs.q: Why does my chameleon need water before it eats?
faqs.a: A chameleon's tongue works when it is hydrated, so water is offered before food to lubricate it. Jackson's chameleons only drink droplets from leaves and surfaces, never from a dish, which is why misting or a dripper comes first and the insects second.

title: How to Handle a Jackson's Chameleon
seoTitle: How to Handle a Jackson's Chameleon Correctly
excerpt: Jackson's chameleons are among the more docile chameleons kept as pets, more laid-back than the veiled chameleon, but docile for a chameleon still means minimal handling.
imageAlt: Male Jackson's chameleon with three forward-facing horns being approached for handling from below
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Are Jackson's chameleons more docile than other chameleons?
faqs.a: Yes, more so than the veiled chameleon. The comparison is relative, though: docile for a chameleon still means an animal you watch rather than hold.

faqs.q: How can you tell a male Jackson's chameleon from a female?
faqs.a: By the horns. Males carry three forward-facing ones, while females have reduced horns or none at all. It makes this one of the few reptiles you can usually sex at a glance.

faqs.q: What stress signals should I watch for when handling one?
faqs.a: Gaping, sunken eyes, a jerking head, rocking or swaying, a curled tail, and front legs raised. Young chameleons run more defensive than adults, and light gloves are reasonable with a feisty one.

faqs.q: What's the biggest first-timer mistake with this species?
faqs.a: Handling too much. Stress here goes past discomfort and can turn dangerous for the animal. Housing two per enclosure is the other one: males fight with those horns.

faqs.q: Do Jackson's chameleons lay eggs like a veiled chameleon?
faqs.a: No. Jackson's chameleons are ovoviviparous, so the female carries the young and gives birth to them live. A single birth runs anywhere from 5 to 30 offspring, after a gestation of roughly 5 to 6 months.

faqs.q: How does handling compare between Jackson's and veiled chameleons?
faqs.a: Jackson's is the calmer of the two, though both are minimal-handling animals. The bigger practical gap is climate: this species needs a meaningfully cooler setup.

title: Common Jackson's Chameleon Health Issues
seoTitle: Jackson's Chameleon Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Jackson's chameleons face many of the same core reptile health risks as the veiled chameleon, with a couple of details specific to this species worth knowing.
imageAlt: Male Jackson's chameleon with three forward-facing horns being examined for early signs of illness
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What is the most common health problem in Jackson's chameleons?
faqs.a: Dehydration. Like most chameleons, Jackson's won't reliably drink from a standing water dish. Sunken eyes and lethargy are the signs. Caught early it's manageable at home by increasing misting and dripper output. See a vet if your chameleon doesn't respond, or shows real lethargy.

faqs.q: What causes metabolic bone disease in this species?
faqs.a: Inadequate calcium, vitamin D3, or UVB exposure. Signs include lethargy, rubbery or bent bones, swollen limbs, and tremors. Always see a vet, early cases respond considerably better to treatment than advanced ones.

faqs.q: What is edema and why is it specific to this species?
faqs.a: Fluid-filled sacs under the throat, neck, or chest, and this species is particularly prone to them. It's often linked to over-supplementing vitamin A or D. See a vet, then review your supplement routine, since more isn't always better here.

faqs.q: What causes gout in Jackson's chameleons?
faqs.a: Chronic dehydration, overfeeding, or a diet too high in protein, which builds up uric acid. Swollen joints are the sign. Always see a vet. Full resolution can be difficult once this develops, so hydration and diet matter more here than treatment.

faqs.q: Why do chameleons need a specific vitamin A source?
faqs.a: They don't convert plant-based beta-carotene very effectively, so the diet needs a source of preformed vitamin A. Signs of a shortfall: eye problems, poor coordination, a weakening grip, and respiratory issues. Always see a vet.

faqs.q: What's the underlying pattern behind most of these issues?
faqs.a: Too little misting leads to dehydration, the most common issue in this species. Weak UVB and calcium lead to MBD. Overfeeding plus dehydration drives gout. Too much vitamin A or D can cause edema. Calibrate hydration and supplementation, don't just provide them.

title: Is It Legal to Own a Jackson's Chameleon? State Guide
seoTitle: Are Jackson's Chameleons Legal? Hawaii Is the Twist
excerpt: Jackson's chameleons clear 46 of 52 jurisdictions, and the one that bars them is the one where they are most abundant. Hawaii's feral population descends from a single 1972 release in Kaneohe, and no private keeper there may hold one.
imageAlt: Male Jackson's chameleon in profile on a branch, all three horns visible
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Where is Jackson's chameleon illegal?
faqs.a: Hawaii and the District of Columbia bar private ownership. New Jersey and West Virginia require a permit, and Minnesota and Maine attach conditions. The other 46 jurisdictions place no restriction on it.

faqs.q: Why is it banned in Hawaii when it lives there?
faqs.a: Because Hawaii's rule is about introduction rather than presence. Introduction is allowed only for animals on its conditionally approved or restricted lists, and this species is on neither, so it is barred by default. The feral population traces to a single 1972 release in Kaneohe and does not change what the lists say.

faqs.q: Does Maine clear chameleons as a family?
faqs.a: No, and that is unusual. Maine lists ten chameleons individually, including two Trioceros, rather than clearing Chamaeleonidae whole. Jackson's chameleon is named, so it is cleared, but a chameleon keeper cannot reason from the family the way they can with geckos or skinks.

faqs.q: Are the horns treated as a dangerous feature anywhere?
faqs.a: No. The three horns on a male are a display and sparring structure, not a defensive weapon against people, and no jurisdiction on this map regulates the species on that basis. The restrictions it does meet are all about introduction or closed permit lists.

title: Jackson's Chameleon Enclosure Setup: Considerably Cooler Than the Veiled Chameleon
seoTitle: Jackson's Chameleon Tank Setup Guide
excerpt: Jackson's chameleon husbandry looks similar to the veiled chameleon's on paper, tall screen enclosure, misting, UVB, but the actual temperature numbers run meaningfully cooler.
imageAlt: Male Jackson's chameleon with three forward-facing horns in a planted, partially screened enclosure
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size enclosure does an adult Jackson's chameleon need?
faqs.a: 24 by 24 by 48 inches for one adult, and bigger is better. A juvenile under about 10 months can sit temporarily in something like 16x16x30. One chameleon per enclosure: males fight.

faqs.q: What temperature does a Jackson's chameleon need, and how does it differ from a veiled chameleon?
faqs.a: Basking near 85°F, much like a veiled chameleon, but the ambient air stays cooler at 68 to 75°F, with a real night drop to 50 to 65°F. Night heat is usually unnecessary and can work against a species adapted to cool mountain nights.

faqs.q: What humidity does this species need?
faqs.a: 60 to 100% relative humidity, the veterinary figure, from misting every 4 to 8 hours or an automated mister, with a cool-mist humidifier where the room cannot hold it. The misting is also how the chameleon drinks. Live plants hold it up naturally.

faqs.q: What substrate and lighting does a Jackson's chameleon need?
faqs.a: Bare bottom with paper towel is simplest, though bioactive works. UVB is required: a Zoo Med ReptiSun 5.0 T5 HO or an Arcadia Forest 6%, swapped every 6 to 12 months.

faqs.q: What are the non-obvious setup requirements for this species?
faqs.a: Two or three solid sides rather than full mesh, which holds humidity and cuts stress. Use distilled water in misters and foggers, disinfect the equipment on a schedule, and never run a fogger while the heat lamp is on, since the combination can create dangerous conditions.

title: Four Pets Content to Stay Out of the Spotlight
seoTitle: Chameleon, Canary, Millipede & Corydoras
excerpt: Every pet category has its showstopper, the veiled chameleon, the talking parrot, the tarantula everyone recognizes, the oscar with a personality. These four are the quieter relatives standing just behind that spotlight, and each one holds up fine on its own terms.
imageAlt: Jackson's chameleon, canary, giant millipede, and corydoras catfish shown side by side
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What makes Jackson's chameleons different from the veiled chameleon?
faqs.a: Quite a bit, despite being commonly grouped together. Jackson's chameleon males grow three forward facing horns, females give live birth to fully formed babies instead of laying eggs, and the species comes from a cooler, higher elevation climate than the veiled chameleon. It's a different animal to house, not just a smaller or quieter version of its more famous cousin.

faqs.q: Do canaries behave like parrots, learning to step up or talk?
faqs.a: No, and that's the point of the species. A canary is a song and observation bird, not a hands on companion bird the way a parrot is. The male's testosterone driven singing is the entire reason people keep this species, not a bonus feature layered onto a parrot style pet.

faqs.q: Are giant millipedes dangerous or venomous?
faqs.a: No. Unlike tarantulas, scorpions, and mantises, a giant millipede can't bite or sting. Its only defense is a mild smelling chemical secretion, and its diet is decaying leaf litter rather than live prey, which makes it arguably the gentlest invertebrate kept as a pet.

faqs.q: How is a corydoras catfish different from a tank centerpiece fish like the oscar?
faqs.a: The oscar demands a big tank and center stage, recognizing its keeper and dominating the glass. The corydoras wants the opposite, six of its own kind, some soft sand, and a quiet corner near the bottom of the tank. It's a social, active little fish, just not one built to dominate a tank the way an oscar does.

faqs.q: Do corydoras catfish need to be kept in groups?
faqs.a: Yes. A corydoras wants six of its own kind at minimum to feel secure and to display natural schooling behavior, not the solo or paired setup that works for some other community fish.

faqs.q: What do these four pets have in common?
faqs.a: None of them are trying to outshine the flashier species in their category, and none of them need to. A cooler, live bearing chameleon, a bird bred for song rather than touch, a harmless plant eating invertebrate, and a schooling fish content to stay in the background. Each one rewards attention precisely because it isn't demanding it.

title: How Much Does a Jumping Spider Really Cost?
seoTitle: Jumping Spider Price: $15 to $60, Plus $112 to $150 Setup
excerpt: Jumping spiders, the regal jumping spider especially, are one of the most affordable and low space pets on this entire site, accessible even on a tight budget.
imageAlt: Regal jumping spider perched near its small vertical enclosure and basic supplies
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a jumping spider cost?
faqs.a: $15 to $60. Captive-bred spiderlings run $15 to $25, while juvenile or sub-adult females, generally more prized since they live considerably longer than males, run $25 to $60. The size gap is small, an adult female averaging 15 mm to a male's 12 mm on the University of Florida's species page; what you are paying for is the lifespan. Named regional color forms cost more than standard animals.

faqs.q: What does a complete jumping spider setup cost upfront?
faqs.a: Roughly $112 to $150, covering a small vertical arboreal enclosure, coconut fiber substrate, artificial plants or cork bark for climbing, a fine mister, and a digital hygrometer. The enclosure is most of it.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing monthly costs of keeping a jumping spider?
faqs.a: About $5 to $15 a month, almost entirely feeder insects, fruit fly cultures for young spiders, and small crickets or fly spikes for adults.

faqs.q: Do jumping spiders need vet care?
faqs.a: Effectively none. Exotic vets rarely treat spiders, and the large majority of problems in this species come from the enclosure environment rather than from anything needing professional treatment.

faqs.q: How long does a jumping spider live, and how does that affect budgeting?
faqs.a: Males typically get 8 to 12 months after maturity, females 1.5 to 3 years. Expect 1 to 3 years overall, which keeps the total cost of ownership small and the commitment short.

title: Jumping Spider Enrichment: They Can Recognize Individuals
seoTitle: Jumping Spider Enrichment Guide
excerpt: A 2024 paper in eLife documented individual recognition in Phidippus regius. This is a spider that learns shapes, avoids places and knows who it has met.
imageAlt: A regal jumping spider on a cork bark flat, front eyes facing the camera
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there real cognition research on jumping spiders?
faqs.a: A surprising amount. There is published work on visual discrimination learning in Phidippus regius, a replication study on shape discrimination conditioning in the same species, a 2024 eLife paper documenting individual recognition in P. regius, and place avoidance learning and memory in another salticid. A 2020 review in Learning and Behavior argues jumping spiders are an exceptional group for comparative cognition.

faqs.q: What does that mean for how I keep one?
faqs.a: That the enrichment axis is visual. Salticids have exceptional vision for their size and navigate complex environments by sight, so structural and visual complexity does more than anything scent or texture based would.

faqs.q: Does captivity change their behavior?
faqs.a: It appears to. Comparisons between lab-reared and field-collected Phidippus audax found differences in color preferences, aggression, courtship and exploratory behavior. That is a captivity effect worth naming honestly in a care guide rather than assuming a captive-bred spider behaves like a wild one.

faqs.q: Should I feed live prey?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the closest thing to a hunting outlet these animals get. Jumping spiders stalk and pounce rather than building capture webs, so live prey that has to be located and pursued engages the behavior the animal is built around.

faqs.q: Do jumping spiders need climbing structure?
faqs.a: Yes. Behavioral enrichment for salticids in the literature is described in terms of climbing and nesting structures such as natural wood branches. They build silk retreats in elevated corners and use vertical surfaces constantly.

faqs.q: Is handling enrichment for a jumping spider?
faqs.a: Interaction with human caretakers during handling and maintenance is mentioned in the literature as a form of behavioral enrichment for salticids, which is unusual for an invertebrate. It should still be brief, low and over a soft surface, because a fall can be fatal.

title: Jumping Spider Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and Why They Stop Eating
seoTitle: What Do Jumping Spiders Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: Let the abdomen do the talking. Here's a real feeding schedule by life stage, safe prey, and how to tell normal premolt fasting from a jumping spider that needs help.
imageAlt: Jumping spider eating a fruit fly on a leaf inside its enclosure
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How often should I feed my jumping spider?
faqs.a: It depends on life stage and varies a fair amount even among adults: spiderlings eat every 1 to 2 days, tapering to roughly every 2 to 5 days by adulthood. The guide is the abdomen, shrunken or wrinkled means feed, plump and noticeably wider than the cephalothorax means skip the next meal.

faqs.q: What should I feed a jumping spider?
faqs.a: Flightless fruit flies for slings and small juveniles, moving up to pinhead crickets, houseflies, and small roach nymphs for juveniles through adults. Flies are a favorite low-risk staple, they can't bite back or burrow into substrate.

faqs.q: What should I never feed a jumping spider?
faqs.a: Ants, above all: jumping spiders show an instinctive fear response to them, and an ant can bite or spray formic acid. Also unsafe are hard-shelled beetles, pill bugs, fireflies, and any prey larger than the spider's own body.

faqs.q: Why has my jumping spider stopped eating?
faqs.a: Most commonly it's premolt fasting, which can last anywhere from a few days to several weeks depending on the spider's size. Post-molt recovery, breeding behavior, and simple prey pickiness are other normal explanations. Real concern shows up as a shrunken, raisin-like abdomen paired with lethargy.

faqs.q: How long can a jumping spider go without eating?
faqs.a: Longer than most people expect, a healthy adult can typically go 2 to 3 weeks without concern, and older adults are anecdotally reported tolerating a month or more, especially around a molt or egg-guarding. There's no true veterinary source for this specific number though, it's hobbyist-reported, not clinically established.

faqs.q: Do jumping spiders need calcium supplements?
faqs.a: No, that's not standard practice for this species the way it is for reptiles. Gut-loading feeder insects on a nutritious diet before offering them is the actual supplementation method used here.

title: How to Handle a Jumping Spider (And Why Its Eyesight Matters)
seoTitle: How to Safely Handle a Jumping Spider
excerpt: Jumping spiders are different from most spiders kept as pets, and that difference starts with how they hunt.
imageAlt: Jumping spider walking onto an owner's hand during a calm, low handling session
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Can you handle a jumping spider?
faqs.a: More readily than most spiders. They're curious, they track movement, and they generally aren't aggressive toward people, with bites that are rare and medically trivial. Minimal handling is still the right default.

faqs.q: What's the right way to handle a jumping spider?
faqs.a: Let it walk onto your hand and off again on its own, without grabbing. Work low and over something soft: these spiders are fragile enough that even a short fall can rupture the abdomen and kill them.

faqs.q: What are the most common handling mistakes with this species?
faqs.a: Dropping or injuring a spider during handling is by far the most common way keepers accidentally harm this species. Using an unmonitored heat mat and letting the enclosure run too dry are the other two common, preventable mistakes.

faqs.q: How is a jumping spider different from a web-building spider?
faqs.a: It hunts by sight instead of by web. Large forward-facing eyes let a jumping spider stalk prey and pounce, sometimes across many times its own body length, while a web builder waits for dinner to arrive.

faqs.q: Do jumping spiders make silk?
faqs.a: Yes, but only for draglines and a small retreat, not for trapping food the way a web-building spider does.

title: Common Jumping Spider Health Issues
seoTitle: Jumping Spider Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Jumping spiders are hardy when humidity stays consistent, and the large majority of health problems in this species trace back to that one factor.
imageAlt: Jumping spider with a healthy, plump abdomen resting near a misted enclosure wall
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What's the most common health problem in pet jumping spiders?
faqs.a: Dehydration, the leading cause of death in captive jumping spiders. Curled legs and lethargy are the signs. The cause is humidity too low, or no drinkable water droplets. Mist the enclosure regularly, and for a spider showing real signs, a damp cotton ball setup can help it recover.

faqs.q: What happens if a jumping spider gets stuck during a molt?
faqs.a: It can lose limbs or die. That is retained molt, or dysecdysis, and it comes from insufficient humidity in the lead-up to the molt. Once a molt has failed, there's little that can be done, so never feed or disturb a spider in or approaching one.

faqs.q: What is silk impaction?
faqs.a: A spider stops producing silk normally. Serious, and often fatal, and it traces to chronic low humidity over time.

faqs.q: Can household chemicals hurt a jumping spider?
faqs.a: Yes. Household sprays and residue from pet flea treatments bring on jerky tremors and loss of coordination, and even indirect contact can affect a spider this small. There's no antidote, so move it to clean air immediately.

faqs.q: Can a jumping spider overheat?
faqs.a: Yes, from direct sun or an unregulated heat mat. Fix the placement, and always run supplemental heat through a thermostat if you use it at all.

title: Jumping Spider Enclosure Setup: Small, Simple, and All About Humidity
seoTitle: Jumping Spider Enclosure Setup Guide
excerpt: Jumping spider setups are small, inexpensive, and simple once you understand the one factor that matters most: keeping humidity consistent.
imageAlt: Small vertical jumping spider enclosure with coconut fiber substrate, climbing branches, and a hygrometer
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What size enclosure does a jumping spider need?
faqs.a: About 4 by 4 by 7 inches, oriented vertically, is the minimum for an adult, and 8 to 10 inches tall gives real climbing room. Arboreal species: height counts for more than floor.

faqs.q: What temperature and humidity does a jumping spider need?
faqs.a: 72 to 82F suits this species well, and normal room temperature is usually fine without any supplemental heat. Target 50 to 60% humidity for Phidippus species like the regal jumping spider, misting one corner every 2 to 3 days with dechlorinated water.

faqs.q: Can I house more than one jumping spider together?
faqs.a: No. House one spider per enclosure, they're cannibalistic toward each other.

faqs.q: What substrate is best for a jumping spider enclosure?
faqs.a: Coconut fiber, or coconut fiber blended with sphagnum moss, an inch or two deep, which buffers humidity between mistings. No sand or vermiculite, and bare paper towel dries out too fast for long-term use.

faqs.q: Does a jumping spider need UVB lighting?
faqs.a: No, UVB is not required for this species. It does need bright ambient light on a normal 12-hour day and night cycle, since it's diurnal and relies on vision to hunt.

title: Is It Legal to Own a California Kingsnake? State-by-State Guide
seoTitle: Is a California Kingsnake Legal in Your State? Full Guide
excerpt: California kingsnakes are legal to own almost everywhere in the US, but Oregon and Nevada both write their rules around how the snake looks rather than what species it is. Hawaii bans every snake outright, and Delaware requires a permit for any reptile not native to the state.
imageAlt: California kingsnake coiled in its enclosure, showing its banded pattern
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Does a kingsnake's color pattern affect its legal status anywhere?
faqs.a: Yes, in two states. Oregon's noncontrolled-species rule only clears kingsnakes that are morphologically distinct from native species, meaning a recognizable color or pattern morph rather than a wild-type-looking snake, a holdover from when the California kingsnake was classified as a subspecies under an older taxonomy. Nevada's unprotected-reptile category specifically singles out California kingsnakes that lack a continuous banded or ringed pattern from head to vent. In both states, what the snake looks like matters as much as what species it is.

faqs.q: Is a California kingsnake legal in Oregon?
faqs.a: It depends on the individual snake. Oregon's rule, OAR 635-056-0060(D), only covers kingsnakes that are morphologically distinct from native species, in practice a recognizable color or pattern morph. An ordinary wild-type-looking California kingsnake or its offspring isn't clearly covered by that clearance, since the rule was written under an older taxonomy and was never updated to name the species outright.

faqs.q: Is a kingsnake banned anywhere in the US?
faqs.a: Yes. Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder Serpentes outright, with no pet-keeping permit available, so a California kingsnake is illegal there the same as any other snake. Delaware doesn't ban it but does require a permit, since it's a reptile not native to or generally found in the state. Those are the only two states that stand in the way anywhere in the country.

title: Four Pets People Get Wrong Before They Even Bring One Home
seoTitle: Koi, Conure, Red-Eared Slider & Emperor Scorpion Myths
excerpt: A pond fish, a parrot, a turtle, and a scorpion, each one gets sold on an assumption that turns out to be backwards once you look at the animal.
imageAlt: Koi, green cheek conure, red-eared slider, and emperor scorpion shown side by side
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Is a green cheek conure a low-maintenance pet because it's quieter than other conures?
faqs.a: Quieter than a sun conure or Jenday conure, yes, but that's not the same as low-maintenance. Green cheek conures are social, intelligent birds that need daily out-of-cage time and real interaction, and a bored, under-stimulated conure gets loud and destructive fast regardless of how quiet the species is on paper.

faqs.q: How much space does an adult red-eared slider need?
faqs.a: Most experienced keepers recommend 75 to 100 gallons or more for a single adult, with 100 to 125 gallons preferred for water quality and swimming room. That's a long way from the small starter tank most hatchlings are sold alongside, which is exactly why so many sliders get outgrown and rehomed.

faqs.q: Are emperor scorpions dangerous to keep?
faqs.a: Not especially. They rely on their large pincers for defense far more than their sting, and a sting from a healthy adult is typically mild, often compared to a bee sting. They're also widely considered the standard beginner recommendation among pet scorpions for exactly this reason.

faqs.q: Why is a koi pond such a bigger commitment than people expect?
faqs.a: Mostly the lifespan. A koi bought as a few inches of color can live 25 to 50 years, and the pond, filtration, and aeration it needs scale up with its size, not the size it was at the pet store. It's more of an infrastructure project than a typical pet purchase.

title: How Much Does Koi Fish Ownership Really Cost?
seoTitle: Koi Fish Price: $10 to $50,000, Plus Pond Setup Costs
excerpt: The fish itself is often the smallest number in the whole equation. Koi ownership is pond ownership, and that's where the budget lives.
imageAlt: Colorful koi swimming in a well-filtered outdoor pond
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How much does a koi fish itself cost?
faqs.a: $10 to $50,000 or more, depending entirely on quality tier. Domestic pond-quality juveniles commonly run $10 to $100. Imports from Japan average roughly $100 to $1,500, show fish $1,200 to $15,000. Champion bloodlines can reach $3,500 to $50,000 or more, and rare auction fish have sold for hundreds of thousands to over a million dollars.

faqs.q: How much does a koi pond setup cost upfront?
faqs.a: Commonly $5,100 to $15,875 for a residential pond of 6x8 to 11x16 feet, holding 1,000 gallons up to several thousand; recent cost analyses average around $10,000. A small prefab can start near $500, and a large custom build can reach $50,000 to $80,000 or more.

faqs.q: What are the ongoing costs of keeping koi?
faqs.a: Commonly $1,000 to $2,000 or more a year. In active season food is $30 to $75 or more a month, and it drops sharply once the water falls below about 48 to 50°F and koi stop eating. Pumps, UV, and aeration run continuously, often another $30 to $80 a month.

faqs.q: Do koi need regular vet visits?
faqs.a: Not typically. Specialized aquatic vets are hard to find, and many keepers handle minor issues with water quality correction and over the counter treatments. Where a vet is available, a routine exam tends to run in the low to mid hundreds, and costs climb fast for a valuable fish or a pond wide problem.

faqs.q: How long do koi live, and why does that matter for budgeting?
faqs.a: 25 to 50 years with good care is the commonly cited range, making koi one of the longest financial commitments in the entire pet world. Japanese bloodlines are often noted as hardier and longer lived than domestic lines, which may average closer to 15 years. Claims of individuals living past 100, most famously a fish named Hanako at a reported 226 years, are popular in the hobby but not independently verified.

title: Koi Enrichment: Volume, Depth, and Somewhere to Overwinter
seoTitle: Koi Enrichment Guide
excerpt: Koi live for decades, reach the length of your arm and learn who feeds them. Nearly every welfare problem they have is a pond that was built too small.
imageAlt: Several large koi rising together toward the surface of a deep planted pond
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there research on koi welfare?
faqs.a: Not in the form of a controlled enrichment study. Koi are carp, one of the most-studied fish groups in aquaculture, and the useful evidence is about space, water quality, stocking density and social behavior rather than about enrichment as such.

faqs.q: How big do koi get?
faqs.a: Around two feet is normal for a well-kept adult and larger is possible. They are sold at a few inches, which is the root of nearly every koi welfare problem: a pond built for the fish in the bag rather than the fish it becomes.

faqs.q: How deep should the pond be?
faqs.a: Deep enough that the bottom does not freeze and stays thermally stable, which in most temperate climates means at least three to four feet in part of the pond. Depth is what makes overwintering survivable rather than merely survivable-looking.

faqs.q: Are koi social?
faqs.a: Yes. They are shoaling fish that feed and move together, and a solitary koi is a poorer arrangement. They also learn a feeding routine and readily learn to take food from a hand.

faqs.q: What is the biggest killer?
faqs.a: Water quality in an overstocked pond, usually in summer when warm water holds less oxygen and a heavy fish load is producing the most waste. Filtration and aeration have to be sized for the adult fish, not the current ones.

faqs.q: Do they need plants?
faqs.a: Plants help with shade, water quality and cover, and koi will eat and uproot them. The usual answer is planting protected in baskets or in a separate shallow zone the fish cannot fully reach.

title: Koi Feeding: Schedule, Diet, and Why They Stop Eating
seoTitle: What Do Koi Eat? Diet and Feeding Schedule
excerpt: Koi feeding is driven almost entirely by water temperature, not the calendar. Here's the seasonal schedule, what to feed, and why stopping feeding in cold water can save a koi's life.
imageAlt: Koi rising to the pond surface to feed on floating pellets
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How often should I feed my koi?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on water temperature, not the season by name. Roughly, stop below 48 to 50°F, feed sparingly once or twice a day between 50 and 68°F, and 2 to 4 times a day in the 68 to 86°F growth range. Above about 86 to 90°F, cut back again, heat stress impairs digestion too.

faqs.q: Why do I need to stop feeding koi in cold water?
faqs.a: Koi have no true stomach, food passes straight into the intestine. If a koi enters cold-water torpor with food still in its gut, undigested material can let harmful bacteria cross the intestinal wall into the bloodstream. Stopping feeding before it gets that cold isn't just a rule of thumb, it's the actual reason koi ponds get into trouble in winter.

faqs.q: How much should I feed at each meal?
faqs.a: The traditional 5-minute rule, only offer what's cleaned up in 3 to 5 minutes, is the most repeated guidance, and it is also the easiest one to overfeed on, since a koi keeps taking food past the point of needing it. A body-weight-based approach, roughly 1 to 4% of body weight a day depending on temperature and size, is the more precise alternative if you want it.

faqs.q: Should I feed a different food in spring and fall?
faqs.a: Yes. A lower-protein wheat-germ formula is easier to digest at low metabolic rates and is the right choice in the 50 to 64°F range. Save the higher-protein warm-season growth and color formula for consistently warmer water above roughly 60 to 64°F.

faqs.q: Why has my koi stopped eating?
faqs.a: In cold water, this is completely normal, koi enter a hibernation-like torpor below about 48 to 50°F and live off stored fat until spring. In warm water, poor water quality is the most common concerning cause, especially if multiple fish stop eating at once, that's a signal to test the water immediately.

faqs.q: How long can a koi go without eating?
faqs.a: In winter, weeks to months is by design and not a red flag. In warm water, koi can go roughly two weeks without dedicated feeding since they forage naturally in the pond, so a few days of reduced eating isn't automatically an emergency. What is concerning: appetite loss lasting more than a few days in warm water, especially paired with sluggishness, color loss, or visible sores.

title: How to "Handle" Koi (Mostly, You Don't)
seoTitle: How to Handle Koi Fish Safely
excerpt: Koi are social, hardy, and food motivated, but this isn't a fish you pick up and hold. Physical handling carries real risk, both to the fish and to you.
imageAlt: Koi being guided into a floating bowl with a net instead of being lifted by hand
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Can you pick up or hold a koi?
faqs.a: Not casually. Contact damages the slime coat that keeps infection out, and a thrashing koi can bruise or injure itself against your hands or the container. Save handling for treatment, transport, or showing.

faqs.q: What's the right way to move a koi?
faqs.a: Net it into a floating bowl or soft container instead of lifting it out. Wet your hands or the towel first, since dry surfaces strip the slime coat, and cradle rather than grip. A sock net or a water filled bag works for transfers.

faqs.q: Do koi have whiskers?
faqs.a: Yes, two pairs of barbels at the corners of the mouth, whisker-like feelers that carry taste and touch receptors for finding food in murky water. Goldfish have none, which makes the barbels the quickest way to tell the two apart at the pond edge.

faqs.q: Do koi bite?
faqs.a: Not in any defensive sense. Koi have pharyngeal teeth used for processing food, not defense, so bites aren't a concern. Look, don't touch, is the practical daily rule with this species.

faqs.q: Are all koi shy around people?
faqs.a: Most are reserved, but Chagoi is the exception. That variety takes to hand feeding and will come to its keeper, friendly enough that enthusiasts compare it to a large, food motivated dog. Don't expect it from the rest of the pond.

faqs.q: What's the biggest handling mistake first time koi keepers make?
faqs.a: Over-handling or rough netting, which strips the slime coat and opens the door to secondary infections. Other common mistakes include handling with dry hands, forcing restraint on a fish that's trying to get away, skipping quarantine for new arrivals, and letting water quality slide, which makes fish skittish or unusually aggressive at feeding time.

title: Common Koi Health Issues (Water Quality Is the Root of Almost Everything)
seoTitle: Koi Health Issues: Signs & Causes
excerpt: Across koi keeping resources, one theme repeats constantly: poor water quality is behind most health problems. Get that right and most of this list never shows up.
imageAlt: Koi pond keeper testing water quality parameters near the pond edge
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: What's the most common cause of koi health problems?
faqs.a: Poor water quality. Ammonia or nitrite that climbs, unstable pH, low oxygen, overcrowding, and sudden changes all stress fish, and stressed fish pick up parasites and bacterial infections. Fixing husbandry solves far more than medication does.

faqs.q: What parasites commonly affect koi?
faqs.a: Ich, Costia, Trichodina, flukes, anchor worm, and fish lice. The signs are flashing or rubbing against pond surfaces, excess mucus, clamped fins, and lethargy. New fish or plants added without quarantine are a common source.

faqs.q: What is koi herpesvirus (KHV) and how serious is it?
faqs.a: The most serious koi disease, causing gill necrosis, excess mucus, lethargy, and skin lesions. Outbreaks can carry mortality rates of 80 to 100%, it's temperature dependent, and there's no reliable cure. Survivors can remain carriers, which is exactly why strict quarantine of 4 to 6 weeks or longer is the critical prevention step.

faqs.q: Can I treat sick koi myself, or do I need a vet?
faqs.a: Many cases are manageable at home, especially mild flashing or early stage parasites with otherwise good water parameters, once water quality is corrected. But specialized aquatic vets are limited in availability, so for valuable fish or any unclear diagnosis, lean toward professional guidance where you can find it.

faqs.q: What's the underlying pattern behind most koi illnesses?
faqs.a: Chronic ammonia and nitrite stress from inadequate filtration, overstocking, or overfeeding, which opens the door to parasites and bacterial ulcers. Skipping quarantine is how parasites and KHV arrive in the first place. Changing water without a conditioner is a fast route to acute toxicity.

title: Koi Pond Setup: Built for Waste Volume, Not Just Water Volume
seoTitle: Koi Pond Setup Guide
excerpt: Koi husbandry is water management at scale. Get the volume, filtration, and depth right, and koi are hardy, low-drama fish.
imageAlt: Outdoor koi pond with visible filtration, aeration, and predator netting
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: How big should a koi pond be?
faqs.a: Plan on roughly 250 gallons per adult, or 10 gallons per inch of body length. The commonly cited practical minimum is 1,000 gallons, which supports only a few fish, so go larger for water stability and healthy growth.

faqs.q: How deep does a koi pond need to be?
faqs.a: 3 feet at minimum, and 3 to 5 feet or more is better. Depth buys temperature stability, protection from predators, and survival through a freezing winter; a shallow pond can freeze solid or overheat, both dangerous.

faqs.q: Do koi need a heater or UVB lighting?
faqs.a: No heater in a temperate outdoor pond; in cold climates a de-icer keeps a section ice-free for gas exchange. No UVB either, since koi don't use it for vitamin D the way many reptiles do, though a UV clarifier is common and useful for algae and pathogens, which is water treatment, not lighting.

faqs.q: What's the part of koi pond setup beginners get wrong most often?
faqs.a: Filtration. Koi are heavy waste producers, and mechanical and biological filtration needs to be robust, oversized relative to what you'd use for an equivalent volume of smaller fish, with strong aeration and oxygenation alongside it.

faqs.q: Can koi live in an indoor aquarium?
faqs.a: Only temporarily. An indoor aquarium can technically hold koi, but matching an adult's volume and industrial-grade filtration indoors is expensive and impractical for most keepers, which is why outdoor ponds are the standard.

title: Koi vs. Goldfish: Which Pond Fish Actually Fits Your Space
seoTitle: Koi vs. Goldfish: Full Comparison
excerpt: Koi or goldfish? The differences in size, species, and whether you need a pond, not just which one is more colorful at the garden store.
imageAlt: A koi and a goldfish side by side for size comparison
author: Michael Ryan

faqs.q: Are koi and goldfish the same species?
faqs.a: No, and this surprises a lot of people. Koi (Cyprinus rubrofuscus) and goldfish (Carassius auratus) are different species in different genera entirely, both members of the minnow family, but not close enough to interbreed and produce viable offspring. Koi descend from the Amur carp, goldfish from the Prussian carp, two separate domestication stories that happen to have produced similarly colorful ornamental fish.

faqs.q: Do I need a pond for koi, or can I keep them in an aquarium?
faqs.a: You need a real pond. Koi grow far too large for aquarium life long-term, a typical adult needs around 250 gallons of space, and most keepers provide that through an outdoor pond rather than any indoor tank. Goldfish are more flexible: fancy varieties do fine in a large aquarium, while common and comet goldfish also thrive in outdoor ponds if you have one.

faqs.q: Which gets bigger, a koi or a goldfish?
faqs.a: Koi, by a wide margin. A typical adult koi reaches 24 to 25 inches, with some approaching 3 feet in ideal conditions. Most goldfish stay in the 4 to 8 inch range, though pond-raised common and comet goldfish can grow larger than the fancy varieties bred for aquariums.

faqs.q: Which lives longer, a koi or a goldfish?
faqs.a: Koi, often considerably. Koi typically live 25 to 50 years, with some individuals reported reaching 100. Goldfish commonly live 10 to 15 years, though well-documented individuals have lived past 40, the record-holding pet goldfish lived to 43.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper to get started with, koi or goldfish?
faqs.a: Goldfish, by a wide margin, mainly because of the housing difference. A goldfish can start in a modest, properly sized aquarium. Koi realistically require building or maintaining an actual outdoor pond with filtration sized for a large, waste-producing fish, a far bigger upfront investment before you even buy the fish.

title: Labrador Enrichment: A Gene Deletion Explains the Appetite
seoTitle: Labrador Enrichment Guide
excerpt: A deletion in the POMC gene makes some Labradors hungrier and heavier. Assistance dogs carry it more often than pets and stay lean anyway, because they work.
imageAlt: A labrador working at a puzzle feeder with its nose, fully absorbed
author: Mike

faqs.q: Is there research explaining why Labradors are so food obsessed?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is unusually specific. Raffan and colleagues at Cambridge found a 14 base pair deletion in the POMC gene in Labrador retrievers, at an allele frequency of around 12 percent, associated with body weight, adiposity and greater food motivation.

faqs.q: How big is the effect?
faqs.a: Each copy of the deletion added about 0.33 standard deviations of body weight, which the authors noted is more than three times the per-allele effect seen at the FTO locus in humans. It is a real effect rather than a curiosity.

faqs.q: Does that mean an overweight Labrador cannot be helped?
faqs.a: No, and the most useful part of the study is why.
